Nobel Peace Prize Goes to Former ICC Judge. The United States imposed new sanctions on the international body in response.

Iran sentences 38-year-old to death as January protest executions mount. Hadi Abbasian, a 38-year-old resident of northeastern Iran, has been sentenced to death by a Revolutionary Court in Bojnurd after being arrested over his support for the nationwide protests in January, according to information obtained by Iran International.

Iran releases cleric who called for replacing Islamic Republic on bail. Iranian authorities have released hardline cleric Mohammad-Bagher Kharrazi on bail after about a month in detention, the judiciary said on Tuesday.

Clothes, diaries, dolls: Iran forces raid slain protesters’ rooms. Clothes, diaries, books and childhood dolls are being taken from the bedrooms of protesters killed in Iran, as security forces extend pressure on families seeking accountability into the most private spaces of their grief nearly nine months after the January 2026 killings.

Tehran police warn cafes over live music, DJs and hookah. Police in Tehran have warned cafes that they could face closure or lose their licenses for hosting live music, using DJs or serving hookah, extending a broader campaign of enforcement against businesses over entertainment, mandatory hijab rules and support for protests.

Houthi gains reversed at Bab al-Mandab, but Iran’s leverage runs deeper. Saudi-backed Yemeni forces on Monday reversed weeks of Houthi gains around Bab al-Mandab, the strategic strait linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, exposing vulnerabilities in the Iran-backed group even as fighting elsewhere showed how far Yemen remains from a decisive shift.

Iranians cross into Armenia to earn what they cannot at home. Economic crisis is driving some Iranians across the border to Armenia for construction, taxi and delivery work, turning a longtime holiday destination into a source of income for families struggling to make ends meet at home.

Three Iranians spied on Iran International journalists in UK, prosecutors say. Three Iranian men spied on Iran International journalists to assist Iranian intelligence services and prepare for serious violence against at least one target, prosecutors told a London court Tuesday.

Iran, US back to ‘square one’ as diplomacy stalls. Rhetoric is hardening on both sides of the Iran-US standoff, with even Iranian analysts traditionally optimistic about diplomacy warning that relations are slipping back to “square one” as military and economic pressure intensifies.

Iran executes nearly two people a week since January protests. Iran has executed nearly two people a week in political and security cases since the January protests, including over protest- and war-related accusations, while another 194 people face death sentences, an Iran International review of cases shows.

‘Hugging actors are married’: Tehran theatre navigates contact restrictions. A theater production in Tehran displayed a notice to spectators before a performance saying two actors who embrace on stage are married, underscoring the restrictions governing physical contact between men and women under the Islamic Republic.

‘Let ’em take out Los Angeles’: Trump’s Iran remarks ignite backlash. President Donald Trump’s suggestion that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego has sparked a backlash from California officials and prompted the White House to insist that he was misunderstood as he defended the mounting costs of the war with Tehran.

How Iran’s 2022 crackdown was coordinated from the top. Iran’s repression of the Woman, Life, Freedom uprising was coordinated from the top through a functioning chain of command linking senior authorities to security forces on the streets, Amnesty International says.

Iran says economy holding up as pressure mounts on oil, rial. Iran’s central bank chief has rejected what he portrays as a US prediction of economic collapse, even as the rial trades near record lows and Iranian oil exports have fallen to zero.

Iran’s own surveys reveal demand for 'fundamental change'. Two surveys emerging from within or around Iran's political establishment paint a bleak picture of public confidence: deep skepticism toward state institutions, single-digit trust in political officials and overwhelming demand for change.

Iran lawmaker named in alleged illegal treasure excavation. A senior hardline Iranian lawmaker has been named in an allegation involving unauthorized excavation for antiquities and treasure, while parliament is also examining a reported excavation case involving an unnamed member of the legislature.

Family of executed January protester says Iran concealed burial site. The family of Alireza Raisi, executed this week over the January protests in Isfahan, still does not know where he was buried after security agents took his father blindfolded to the burial site, a source close to the family told Iran International.

Iran protester recounts torture, mock execution after January arrest. “Write your will.” Those were the words Iranian protester Erfan Nabian says he heard in solitary confinement before he was handed a sheet of paper and asked what he wanted for his final meal before his execution.

Parsian Exchange transferred millions of dollars for Iran despite sanctions. Iran’s Bank Parsian, under US sanctions, used its foreign-exchange arm to move millions of dollars abroad through a network of intermediaries, according to an Iran International investigation based on leaked internal correspondence and transaction records.

Rubio says Iran missed deal chances as Tehran digs in on enrichment. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday that Iran had failed to take advantage of repeated opportunities to reach an agreement with Washington over its nuclear program, while also saying Tehran had “lost complete control” of the Strait of Hormuz.

Tehran divided over $2 billion plan to prop up rial. Iran’s central bank is offering as much as $2 billion in cash dollars to the public in an effort to slow the rial’s slide, triggering a fierce debate over whether the intervention can stabilize the currency or merely burn through increasingly scarce foreign reserves.

China shifts to Iraqi oil: is Iran using old workaround to beat US blockade?. China’s independent refiners are turning to Iraqi crude to replace dwindling Iranian supplies as a US blockade chokes Tehran’s exports, raising questions about whether Iran is using an old workaround to reach its buyers: disguising its own oil as Iraqi.

Kayhan attacks Ghalibaf’s role in talks. Didn’t Khamenei approve it?. An editorial questioning Mohammad-Bagher Ghalibaf’s role as Iran’s lead negotiator has raised an awkward question in Tehran: who exactly is Kayhan criticizing, given that senior officials have said the parliament speaker was given the job with the Supreme Leader’s approval?

‘$100k-a-month captains’: What it costs to move oil through Hormuz. Oil tanker captains are being paid as much as $100,000 a month and offered $50,000 bonuses for individual trips through the Strait of Hormuz, the latest sign of the extraordinary costs now required to keep crude moving through the waterway since the Iran war began.

Iran looks for escape routes as US sanctions close in. The widening reach of US sanctions across Iran’s transport and industrial networks has raised alarms in Tehran that Washington is seeking to close off the alternative trade routes the country has relied on to circumvent years of economic pressure.

From talks to war: Tehran sees the gap narrowing. Fears of renewed war with the United States, Israel or both are growing in Iran, as military officials talk openly about pre-emptive action and analysts warn that the distance between diplomacy and another round of fighting is becoming dangerously short.

Hezbollah recruitment network in Iran exposed, four safe houses identified. Hezbollah’s external operations unit has been recruiting foreign nationals in Iran and using safe houses in Qom and Tehran to train and shelter recruits, according to information obtained by Iran International.

Islamic Republic supporters take weapons home after training, citizens say. Some participants in military training programs for supporters of the Islamic Republic, including Basij militia members and seminary students, have been allowed to take weapons home, citizens told Iran International, as authorities expand firearms training to schools across Iran.

Police officer killed in armed attack near Zahedan as violence continues in southeast Iran. An Iranian police officer was killed on Thursday when gunmen attacked a patrol near Zahedan in Sistan-Baluchestan, the latest in a series of deadly attacks and clashes involving security forces in southeastern Iran.

Iran's reported $200 million Hezbollah aid angers cash-strapped citizens. Reports that the Islamic Republic sent $200 million to Lebanon's Hezbollah have drawn anger from Iranians struggling with rising living costs, low wages and medicine shortages, according to messages sent to Iran International.

Three years after October 7, Iran pays the price of miscalculation. Three years after Hamas's October 7 attack on Israel, the Islamic Republic faces a weakened network of regional allies, direct military confrontation and mounting economic pressure, upending its long-held strategy of deterring enemies while keeping war away from its territory.

US sanctions 17 ships in push to shut down Iran’s shadow fleet. The US Treasury sanctioned 17 vessels and their owners Thursday under Operation Economic Outcast, saying the action effectively neutralizes most of Iran’s remaining shadow fleet.

Saudi Aramco hires US firm to upgrade shared oil field as Iran lags behind. Saudi Aramco has hired a US engineering firm to upgrade an offshore oil field it shares with Iran, which has fallen far behind several neighbors in developing shared energy reserves.

Trump rules out Iran attack before midterms, Tehran says ready for prolonged war. US President Donald Trump said Thursday the United States would not attack Iran before the November 3 midterm elections and that "productive" talks were underway, after reports of US preparations for possible large-scale strikes.

US pressure hits Iranians harder than rulers, 68% in poll say. More than two-thirds of respondents to an Iran International Instagram poll said the Trump administration’s pressure on the Islamic Republic is hurting ordinary Iranians more than the authorities.

Taliban-run Afghanistan could get ‘land of its own’ on Iran’s coast, MP says. Iran has reached a preliminary understanding to allocate land at Chabahar to Taliban-run Afghanistan to build infrastructure for moving its goods to the sea, an Iranian lawmaker said.

Iraq creates PMF unit to take faction drones as arms plan advances - Erem News. Iraq has created a specialized unit within the Popular Mobilization Forces to take control of drones held by armed factions as part of Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi’s plan to bring weapons under state authority, Erem News reported on Friday, citing an Iraqi security source.

Iranian security forces face wave of deadly attacks in restive southeast. At least five Iranian military and police personnel were killed and several others wounded in four armed attacks across southeastern Iran within 24 hours, local rights group Haalvsh reported, as violence targeting security forces continued across the area.

Iran-origin campaign targeted Iran International, foreign media - OpenAI. An Iran-origin influence operation used fake Western journalist identities to place nearly 100 articles in online news outlets around the world and repeatedly generated hostile social media responses to Iran International, OpenAI said in a report released on Thursday.

Two men deny spying for Iran on Israeli embassy in London. Two men accused of carrying out surveillance on the Israeli Embassy, Britain’s oldest synagogue and other Jewish and Israeli-linked sites in London on behalf of Iran pleaded not guilty on Friday.

UK court hears how alleged Iran spy operation targeted Iran International. Men accused of spying for Iran exchanged information about Iran International’s offices and presenter Kambiz Hosseini, while one defendant discussed money transfers and his legal troubles with contacts in Iran, a London court heard.

Iran turns on Pakistan as Saudi defense pact takes effect. Iran has sharpened its criticism of a Saudi Arabia-Pakistan-Turkey defense pact after it became operational, warning against intervention in Yemen and questioning Pakistan’s role as a mediator between Tehran and Washington.

Teenage boy dies in custody after beating by Iran's Basij forces, source says. A 17-year-old boy died in custody in Iran’s Isfahan province after the IRGC’s paramilitary Basij forces beat him during his arrest and a judge refused his father’s plea for hospital treatment, a source familiar with the case told Iran International.

J’Accuse! Tehran defends French students, silences Iranian youth. Tehran has seized on protests by French high school students to accuse Paris of repression, seeking to obscure its own treatment of young Iranians by turning the language of human rights against one of its Western critics.

Iran executed over 2,000 people in past year, rights group says. Iran executed at least 2,003 people over the past year, a 29% increase from the previous period, rights group HRANA reported Friday, as UN experts warned that Tehran uses capital punishment to silence dissent and instill fear.

'Three golden weeks': Trump’s no-strike pledge fuels calls in Iran to act first. President Donald Trump’s pledge not to attack Iran before the November 3 US midterm elections has been greeted in Tehran as either a bluff or an opportunity, with some hardliners urging Iran to exploit the three-week window to strike first.

Iran-linked actors used US AI for fake journalism, military targeting. Iran-based and Iranian-linked actors have used two leading US artificial intelligence platforms to place articles under fake journalist identities and help develop targeting recommendations against US naval forces, according to separate investigations by OpenAI and Anthropic.

Bessent outlines US plan to cut off Iran’s remaining economic lifelines. The United States is expanding its economic campaign against Iran beyond oil exports and financial sanctions, targeting Tehran’s overland trade routes, Iran-linked cryptocurrency and remaining shipping network, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said this week.

Iran turns to Turkey, Turkmenistan for power as war strains industry. Iran is seeking more electricity from Turkey and Turkmenistan as war damage and other outages leave thousands of megawatts of industrial and petrochemical power capacity offline, even as Washington presses neighboring countries to help restrict Tehran’s remaining economic routes.

Iran detains football coach over child sexual abuse allegations. Iranian judicial authorities have detained a football coach in the western city of Divandarreh after five people filed complaints alleging sexual abuse connected to a youth football club.

Jailed wife of executed Iran protester pressured to deny marriage. The jailed wife of an Iranian protester executed this week is being interrogated and pressured to deny that the couple married shortly before his execution, a source familiar with the case told Iran International.

Loi anticorruption en RDC : Guillaume Ngefa a-t-il les moyens de ses ambitions ?. Présenté le 28 septembre à l’Assemblée nationale, le projet de loi porté par le ministre de la Justice promet de moderniser la lutte contre la corruption. Reste à savoir s’il pourra réussir dans un domaine où son prédécesseur avait lui-même promis d’agir.

Pourquoi la vente d’Oragroup est devenue une course contre la montre vitale. En quête d’une recapitalisation cruciale, le groupe bancaire panafricain a réuni son conseil d’administration le 7 octobre. En vente depuis 2019, la banque est contrainte de réduire ses octrois de crédits pour assurer sa survie.

Prétoires, pouvoir et réseaux : ces avocats qui façonnent la politique ivoirienne. Habiba Touré, Jean-Chrysostome Blessy, Abdoulaye Meïté… En Côte d’Ivoire, les robes noires s’imposent au premier rang des batailles de partis, au sein desquels ils sont militants ou responsables. Le Palais de justice d’Abidjan est ainsi devenu le nouveau théâtre des luttes de pouvoir.

Présidentielle au Cameroun : quand Anicet Ekane attendait Issa Tchiroma Bakary à Yaoundé. En octobre 2025, l’activiste aujourd’hui décédé a été l’un des principaux soutiens du candidat à la présidentielle. Pourtant, leur alliance face à Paul Biya ne s’est pas déroulée comme prévu.

L’Égypte parviendra-t-elle à contenir l’Éthiopie ?. Le Caire tente de rassembler autour de lui les adversaires de l’Éthiopie, mais on ignore encore quelle est la solidité de l’alliance qu’il a nouée avec l’Érythrée, le Soudan et la Somalie, et quelle sera la réaction de Washington.

Hôtellerie : au Sahel, les acteurs se réinventent sans les ONG ni la clientèle étrangère. Privés d’une partie de leur clientèle internationale par la crise sécuritaire et le recul de l’aide au développement, les hôtels sahéliens repensent leurs offres. De Bamako à Ouagadougou, ils tentent de séduire la clientèle locale.

« C’est le moment de rendre les armes » : à Bissau, le général N’Tam lance un appel aux militaires restés proches d’Embaló. Après l’annonce de la candidature à la présidentielle du président déchu Umaro Sissoco Embaló, se sont ensuivies des rumeurs de mécontentement au sein de la garde présidentielle. Dans la foulée, plusieurs éléments ont été désarmés et placés sous contrôle de l’état-major.

Burkina Faso : 10 choses à savoir sur le général Diaouari, le maître à penser sécuritaire d’Ibrahim Traoré. Très proche du président burkinabè, qui l’a élevé au rang de général en juillet dernier, cet officier au profil de technocrate est devenu central dans le dispositif d’Ibrahim Traoré. Des questions sécuritaires à la communication, en passant par la mise en œuvre du souverainisme économique, il est l’un des stratèges de la junte.

Sénégal : le calendrier de la restructuration de la dette est-il crédible ?. Dakar vise un premier soutien du FMI dès le mois de novembre avant de boucler un accord sur sa dette avec les créanciers en décembre. Mais le calendrier semble particulièrement serré.

Le Maroc, porte d’entrée des industries de défense émiraties sur le continent. La présence massive des fournisseurs émiratis de matériel militaire au Marrakech Air Show n’est qu’une manifestation d’un phénomène plus large. Pour Abou Dhabi, le Maroc est plus qu’un marché, c’est aussi un pays stratégique pour séduire les armées de tout le continent.

RDC : Félix Tshisekedi sollicite l’aide de la Monusco pour la démobilisation des FDLR. Le président congolais a écrit au secrétaire général des Nations unies pour qu’il soutienne son plan de démobilisation des anciens génocidaires hutu. La proposition pourrait être étudiée dans le cadre du renouvellement du mandat de la Monusco.

Pour Airtel Money, l’entrée en Bourse est aussi un moyen de relancer les acquisitions. Valorisé 7 milliards de dollars, le géant de la finance mobile s’apprête à faire son entrée à la Bourse de Londres. Elle offre au groupe une vitrine boursière pour mener la consolidation de la fintech en Afrique et convertir ses 75 millions de clients télécoms.

Saddam Haftar : du Sahel au Tchad, les limites d’une diplomatie sécuritaire. Entre libérations d’otages, soutien à des mouvements rebelles et nouvelle alliance avec le Tchad, l’héritier du maréchal Haftar cherche à s’imposer comme un interlocuteur incontournable. Et se rêve en futur président d’une Libye réunifiée qui pèserait de nouveau sur la diplomatie continentale.

Au Cameroun, Maurice Kamto tente la stratégie de l’éminence grise. Alors que le MRC s’apprête à désigner son successeur lors d’une convention toujours contestée, l’opposant reste présent en coulisses. En retrait, il travaille à l’implantation nationale du parti et veut peser sur ses futures alliances électorales.

Pétrole : les dessous de l’incursion manquée de Simon Tiemtoré dans l’aval africain. Le banquier américano-burkinabé s’était positionné, via Lilium Capital Group, pour l’acquisition d’un réseau de quelque 400 stations-service. Mais les discussions n’ont finalement pas abouti. Coulisses.

Prix Nobel de la paix : Navi Pillay, la juriste sud-africaine qui a dénoncé le génocide à Gaza. La juge de 85 ans a consacré sa carrière à qualifier juridiquement les crimes contre l’humanité et les génocides comme à Gaza, au Myanmar ou au Rwanda. Elle rejoint la prestigieuse liste de nobélisés sud-africains.

James Mwangi (Equity) : « L’Afrique doit ajouter de la valeur à ce qu’elle produit ». Expansion régionale, IA et projet de raffinerie à Lamu : le patron du groupe kényan Equity, leader en Afrique de l’Est, met en avant sa stratégie pour assurer l’essor et la diversification de ses activités. Tout en insistant sur la nécessité pour le continent de mieux maîtriser ses chaînes de valeur.

Détention d’Alain-Claude Bilie-By-Nze au Gabon : les coulisses d’un dossier sensible. L’ancien Premier ministre et opposant au président Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema est toujours incarcéré à la prison centrale de Libreville dans l’attente de son procès. Ses conseils fustigent une procédure judiciaire gelée et dénoncent une arrestation politique, ce que réfutent les autorités.

Maroc : avant le discours du roi, où en sont les négociations pour former une coalition ?. Les tractations conduites par Fatima-Ezzahra El Mansouri dessinent les contours possibles d’une majorité articulée autour du PAM et des trois partis historiques de la Koutla. Mais les consultations se poursuivent et d’autres options restent ouvertes.

Pénuries d’essence au Niger : le patron de la compagnie pétrolière nationale paye le prix de la crise. Le chef de la junte au Niger a démis de ses fonctions le patron de Sonidep. Ce limogeage sans explication intervient alors que le pays fait face à de vives tensions sur le carburant.

Les relations Algérie-Espagne à l’épreuve de l’affaire Ayoub Aissiou. Malgré le soutien de Madrid à la demande algérienne, la justice espagnole a refusé l’extradition de l’homme d’affaires, enrichi sous la présidence Bouteflika. Une décision qui pourrait peser sur les relations entre les deux pays.

FMI-Cemac : le Tchad, victime collatérale de la lenteur des réformes communautaires ?. Un an après la signature de son accord avec le FMI, N’Djamena n’a perçu aucun décaissement. L’institution financière conditionne ses versements à des engagements accrus de la part des membres de l’organisation régionale. Coulisses.

En Mauritanie, le gouvernement démissionne après la présentation d’un rapport d’enquête sur des incendies. En août dernier, deux incendies ont touché des infrastructures de la Somelec, privant Nouakchott de courant. Un rapport sévère a coûté sa survie au gouvernement de Mokhtar Ould Djiay.

Pétrole : comment Aliko Dangote est-il devenu le roi du raffinage africain ?. Alors que la crise géopolitique suit son cours au Moyen-Orient, la raffinerie du groupe Dangote à Lekki s’est hissée au rang de fournisseur majeur de carburants pour les marchés internationaux. Une réussite qui peut en appeler une autre, mais dans quelles conditions ?

Sénégal : Ousmane Sonko peut-il (vraiment) utiliser sa majorité à l’Assemblée contre Bassirou Diomaye Faye ?. Les lois votées par le groupe Pastef sont systématiquement bloquées par l’exécutif. Mais les députés de la majorité ont d’autres moyens d’utiliser leur tribune politique.

En Côte d’Ivoire, une affaire d’escroquerie impliquant des influenceurs révèle les failles du foncier. Une soixantaine de plaintes, plus de 320 millions de F CFA de préjudice provisoire et plusieurs célébrités citées : la vaste enquête visant la promotrice Rita Djédjé éclaire les risques qui continuent de peser sur les acquisitions immobilières. Décryptage.

RDC : Kabila règle ses comptes avec Tshisekedi et entretient le mystère sur ses intentions. L’ex-président congolais s’est une nouvelle fois exprimé, le 9 octobre, pour attaquer le bilan de son successeur tout en promettant, « dans les heures, les jours et les semaines à venir », d’annoncer des actions concrètes pour « sauver » le pays.

L’accès à la mer Rouge est-il le véritable enjeu de la guerre entre l’Éthiopie et l’Érythrée ?. Quatre ans après avoir combattu côte à côte lors de la guerre du Tigré, les armées d’Abiy Ahmed et d’Issayas Afewerki s’affrontent dans le nord de l’Éthiopie. Jusqu’où cette escalade pourrait-elle aller ? Décryptage.

Denise Dusauchoy au secret à Kinshasa, le Maroc face à la rupture Algérie-Émirats arabes unis, le calendrier serré de la dette du Sénégal… Les 5 infos qu’il ne fallait pas manquer. Cette semaine, le Brief de Jeune Afrique revient sur la chute de l’influenceuse congolaise Denise Dusauchoy, décrypte les ambitions sahéliennes de Saddam Haftar, s’intéresse aux avocats qui s’imposent dans les batailles politiques ivoiriennes, analyse les conséquences de la rupture entre l’Algérie et les Émirats arabes unis pour le Maroc et évalue la crédibilité du calendrier de restructuration de la dette sénégalaise.

Tramadol en Afrique : le filon des trafiquants, l’antidouleur des pauvres. 97 % des saisies mondiales de tramadol ont lieu en Afrique de l’Ouest et en Afrique centrale. Ce trafic prospère sur un terreau : une région où l’on manque de presque tout pour soulager la douleur. Décryptage en infographies.

Dans la Somalie en guerre, une aide humanitaire empêchée, des populations menacées de famine. Les violents combats entre factions gouvernementales rivales aggravent encore la crise alimentaire qui touche près de sept millions de Somaliens. Fuyant la sécheresse et la faim, les réfugiés ne cessent d’affluer dans les camps où se trouvent les organisations humanitaires, bannies de certaines zones par le mouvement islamiste chabab.

Au Mali, l’armée signe une rare victoire après la prise de la ville stratégique de Kidal, désertée par les rebelles. Cette annonce de la reprise de cette ville devenue un bastion de la rébellion touareg intervient après une série de revers pour l’armée malienne.

Au Mali, la junte regagne du terrain en reprenant Kidal, fief des rebelles touareg. Les militaires maliens et leurs alliés russes avaient été chassés de la ville du Nord le 25 avril, durant l’offensive conjointe des indépendantistes du Front de libération de l’Azawad et des djihadistes du Groupe de soutien de l’islam et des musulmans.

Le journaliste nigérien Moussa Kaka est « en vie » et « détenu » par les autorités, selon Reporters sans frontières. Le sort du journaliste, directeur d’une télévision privée, suscitait de nombreuses inquiétudes depuis sa disparition, le 31 août.

« La France doit accorder l’asile au lanceur d’alerte et journaliste Ephrem Yalike-Ngonzo ». Dans une tribune au « Monde », Reporters sans frontières, le réseau Forbidden Stories et la Plateforme de protection des lanceurs d’alerte en Afrique exhortent les autorités françaises à octroyer l’asile au journaliste centrafricain, source exclusive d’une enquête sur la machine de propagande russe en Afrique.

Des troupes érythréennes sont entrées en Ethiopie, laissant craindre un affrontement direct avec Addis-Abeba. L’armée d’Asmara soutient les insurgés du Front populaire de libération du Tigré, en lutte contre le gouvernement central éthiopien. Des camions militaires et des équipements lourds érythréens ont été aperçus sur le territoire éthiopien.

En Egypte, les six journalistes du média d’investigation « Matsadaash » inculpés d’infractions liées au terrorisme. Les membres de la rédaction du site spécialisé dans le fact-checking avaient été arrêtés fin septembre lors d’un coup de force inédit contre des journalistes.

Finale de la CAN 2025 : le Tribunal arbitral du sport appelé à trancher entre le Maroc et le Sénégal. Pour avoir quitté la pelouse afin de dénoncer un penalty, les Sénégalais ont été déclarés forfaits malgré leur victoire face aux Marocains (1-0). Pezeshkian pitches 'CIS + Iran' bloc at Turkmenistan summit Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has called for a new “CIS + Iran” format, using his first appearance as a special guest at the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) summit in Turkmenistan to pitch Tehran as the region’s gateway to open waters, Tasnim news agency reported. Speaking at the gathering, Pezeshkian said that war, external pressure and disrupted trade routes make regional resilience more urgent than ever. He said Iran is not just a partner but a “natural route” to the sea for Central Asia. Iran’s southern ports, notably Chabahar, he said, could link the region to South Asia, Africa and Europe. “Our common interests lie not in competition among routes, but in connecting them,” he said. He also backed Turkmenistan’s UN proposal for a Caspian Sea transport corridor linking Central Asia, South Asia and Europe, saying it could be built using Iranian infrastructure, according to Tasnim. Pezeshkian used the platform to condemn US and Israeli attacks on Iran, while reiterating Tehran remained open to dialogue, but on one condition: “Negotiation under the shadow of force is not negotiation; it is imposition and coercion.” Sanctions, he warned, would harm not only Iran but regional trade, energy and connectivity, the report said.

Increased vessel attacks drive Hormuz oil exports 'sharply lower', report says Hormuz oil exports were “sharply lower,” falling to a seven-day average of 9.9 million barrels per day as of October 7, 42 percent below prewar levels and down from about 15.5 million in September, according to Kpler data cited by the Financial Times. Kpler said that flows had recovered to prewar levels in September but "intensified attacks on vessels" had driven exports "sharply lower" this week. Energy analyst Rory Johnston also said that the latest estimate puts Hormuz seven-day average oil flow peaking at 16.2 mbpd on September 24. "Then Iran really picked up its shipping attacks and that flow unsurprisingly pulled back by 3-4 mbpd," he wrote on X. "Now seeing flow at 12-13 mbpd over the past two weeks."

Yousof Azizi: The Iranian-American scholar pressured by the FBI to return to Iran Submitted by Amara Sophia Elahi on Thu, 10/01/2026 - 09:19 The political commentator is one of several Iranians whose repatriation may have been coordinated with an ICE official based in Israel Yousof Azizi was detained for three months before requesting voluntary departure from the US to Iran (supplied/MEE) Off Monday 13 April started as a normal day for Yousof Azizi, a PhD student at Virginia Tech University in America. In the morning, he took his 12-year-old daughter and a four-year-old son to their schools in Baltimore, Maryland, before returning home. A vocal opponent of the war on Iran , he had been living in the US for nearly 13 years and was recognised as a prominent political commentator on Persian-language media platforms and on his YouTube channel, which has more than 68,000 subscribers. Azizi had also been involved in discussions with Congress in relation to the Iran nuclear deal during Barack Obama’s presidency. When he arrived back home that April morning, a number of FBI vehicles were parked outside his residence. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Upon exiting his car, Azizi found himself surrounded by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, their rifles pointing straight at him. Basij claims and visa issues Azizi was taken to a detention centre in Baltimore. “The first thing they said to me was that they believed I had been part of the student Basij between 2007 and 2010 when I was studying my master's at Sharif University of Technology in Iran,” Azizi told Middle East Eye. Yousof Azizi was given this document by US authorities as he left the United States (supplied by Yousof Azizi/MEE) The Basij is the volunteer paramilitary branch of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) and functions as a local-level enforcement agency, patrolling the streets and ensuring compliance with the country’s Islamic laws. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The US designated Basij a terrorist entity in 2019, and any Iranians who have served in the force and are applying for American visas are required to declare it on their applications. “I told them I had never been part of the Basij,” Azizi said. “They said they have multiple sources for this, but during my detention and the court proceedings they never presented any evidence to support their claims.” Azizi and his wife had never had any issues previously with American authorities. “The FBI even told the court that I had no criminal record and had never committed any wrongdoing,” he said. As well as accusing Azizi of being in the Basij, the FBI and Department of Homeland Security also claimed that his student visa status had been terminated after he failed to re-enrol for the fall 2025 semester at Virginia Tech. He maintained that he had applied for a change in status so that he could study part time, in order to make his university fees more affordable. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Azizi told MEE he had been questioned by the FBI about this two months before his arrest. “They talked to me for a couple of hours and asked me if my application was rejected would I leave the United States - I said yes,” Aziz said. He also said the FBI called his wife in March asking similar questions, and that a special agent texted him a few days before his arrest asking to meet with him in another city to answer questions. “I texted him back asking him to get in touch with my lawyer if he had further questions, because my university advised me that this might be a scam,” Azizi said. Handcuffed and shackled During his time in detention, Azizi was moved around various facilities across the country. He was transferred from the Baltimore ICE facility to Louisiana, then Arizona, before being taken to the California City processing centre. He said his wife had sought help from NGOs and members of Congress, who told her that he should not have been legally transferred from Baltimore because his spouse and children were there. Aziz described harsh conditions during his detention, saying: “I was handcuffed, there was a chain around my waist which my arms were attached to, and my ankles were shackled. “It was physically very painful. I had to sit like that for 13 days,” he added. “In Arizona we were held for 48 hours in a very cold, small room. There were 20 of us and we were all shaking. “We had to sleep there with no bedding or pillows and no proper clothes, and had to crawl over each other just to get to the toilet. “By the time we got to California most people were ill.” Azizi also said he was denied pain medication for headaches while he was in detention. 'They wanted to get rid of me' Azizi strongly believes his arrest was politically motivated. “Some of the questions I was asked during my detention were on the one hand silly but also show they wanted something else from me - for example, they asked me whether Iran was capable of putting mines in the Strait of Hormuz,” he said. Homeland Security: Two decades of terrorising people of colour Read More » “How could I know this? They have the CIA and surveillance, so they should know. “They also told me they’d watched my YouTube channel and questioned where the transcripts and data I presented in my videos were coming from. They accused me of getting these through connections in Iran.” Azizi told the FBI that the data he used in his videos came from his own research and was publicly available, but that they nevertheless insisted it had come from Iran. He was told that he would be released if he cooperated with the authorities, but said he had nothing to tell them. During his detention, he recounted, he was visited by the head of the Iranian Interests Section at the Pakistani embassy in the US, who told him the FBI had a list of 25 Iranians they deemed a security risk and wanted to remove from the country - Aziz was one of them. “I think they needed some information about Iran, and my videos caused the FBI to focus on my case, and they just wanted to get rid of me,” he said. 'I have to focus on my life in Iran' In June, Azizi decided to request voluntary departure from the US back to Iran. At his most recent bond hearing, the FBI presented a dossier of allegations, reiterating its previous claims and pointing to a clip of Azizi from a media interview that had been circulated on the IRGC’s Telegram channel. “I didn’t send the clip to the IRGC. I had many interviews with a variety of news outlets, many of which are actually banned in Iran, but someone in the IRGC picked up one of my clips and shared it,” Azizi explained. He added that the FBI had characterised him as a flight and national security risk, an accusation he described as baseless. Azizi had 250 letters of support from university professors across the US, but they ultimately made no difference to his case, even as his lawyer staunchly defended him. He said that waiting for a final court hearing could have taken up to two years, with no guarantee of a favourable outcome. A deportation order could have ultimately put his future at risk. On 30 June, Azizi, along with his wife and children, left the US and made his way back to Iran via Turkey. For now, he plans to complete his dissertation from Iran and currently has no plans to return to the US. “I have to focus more on my life in Iran, with my parents, who are over 80 years old, and my children, who know our culture here in Iran,” Azizi said. “I think America wants a single narrative on Iran from the Iranian diaspora and wants to get rid of other voices who are against the war. “I don’t know if this is motivated by Israel, or by Iranian opposition groups in the United States who have targeted me recently.” 'An act to silence somebody' The National Iranian American Council (NIAC), a non-profit organisation that advocates for the rights of Iranian-Americans while promoting diplomatic engagement and opposing war between the US and Iran, supported Azizi during his detention. “Our involvement in these cases is to make sure people have access to the resources necessary for them to protect themselves and to not be exploited because we know of so many cases where it’s a complete black box - nobody can tell what is happening or what their fate is going to be,” NIAC's president, Jamal Abdi, told MEE. “It seems like in Yousof’s case there was potentially a political dimension to the effort to deport him, more so than what already exists in this highly political environment where Iranians are being targeted by ICE for detainment and deportation. 'America wants a single narrative on Iran from the Iranian diaspora and wants to get rid of other voices who are against the war' - Yousof Azizi “It seemed particularly galling that he was detained given the fact he was a prominent commentator, somebody whose research and analysis was featured on television and in print news, and it was hard not to see this as potentially an act to silence somebody whose politics didn't align with the Trump administration.” Other Iranians living in the US have been similarly targeted by the administration on political grounds. Hamideh Soleimani Afshar and her daughter Sarinasadat Hoseiny were arrested by ICE on 3 April and remain in custody. Right-wing media personality Laura Loomer alleged that the women were relatives of former Iranian military general Qassem Soleimani, who was assassinated in a US drone strike in 2020. However, the familial connection remains disputed. Nevertheless, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio repeated Loomer’s claims and argued that Afshar’s Green Card was revoked because she publicly supports the Iranian government. “We know other people, university professors for example, who have been detained and in some cases were let go because ICE didn’t have anything on them. But with Yousof it seems like he was detained and then they found something or came up with some pretext that was never proven,” Abdi observed. “It’s like lawfare where wealthy entities will launch lawsuits, not because they think they can win on the merits but because they think they can bury you in the cost and the resources as it’s not a fair matchup. “It’s sort of similar if you throw someone in a detention centre that is dirty and they don’t have access to food or a bathroom, are moved around the country with no certainty as to when they will ever get their day in court or if there’s a light at the end of the tunnel. A lot of people will say, ‘Fine, I’ll go back to my country of origin.’ I think that’s what Yousof faced.” Questions over role of ICE in Israel A recent investigation by NIAC has revealed that an ICE official based at the US Embassy in Tel Aviv was involved in the deportation of dozens of Iranians in America. Some of these individuals were vulnerable people seeking asylum because of their political views and religious backgrounds. 'The decision to send those people back was made as the US and Israel were bombing Iran' - Jamal Abdi, NIAC president NIAC has published nearly 300 pages of email correspondence between ICE officials that it obtained through Freedom of Information requests, showing that the attache in Israel was working to coordinate deportation flights for Iranians in 2025. The order to begin deporting Iranians came directly from the White House in June 2025, around the time of the 12-day US-Israeli war on Iran. According to NIAC’s data, 418 Iranians were detained by ICE between June 2025 and December 2025, with 300 arrested in June and July of that year. Meanwhile, 125 Iranians were deported to Iran on three flights between the end of September 2025 and January 2026. Although ICE has an international presence, Abdi believes the extent of this Tel Aviv official’s involvement in Iranian deportations is particularly significant. “It's a post that has more heft to it than some of the other ICE attaches around the world,” he observed. “We know that there have been past instances regarding Palestinian deportations where Israel has been involved, but this struck us as worthy of further investigation.” The situation has raised questions about how susceptible ICE is to pressure from the Israeli government, given the influence of Israeli lobby groups in the US. 'Bloodline punishment': Iranian family faces ongoing punitive ICE detention Read More » Abdi said that Israel has devoted significant resources to targeting the Iranian diaspora through propaganda. He pointed to campaigns led by former Israeli Intelligence Minister Gila Gamliel that involved using bots and other inauthentic online activity to influence Persian-speaking audiences and promote Israeli policies and positions towards Iran, as reported by Haaretz newspaper. Abdi told MEE that Americans deserve answers as to why ICE exists in Israel, and whether there is coordination between the US and Israel to target people in the country. In a statement to MEE, the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) denied any Israeli involvement in the deportation of Iranians from the US. "ICE HSI has attaches stationed around the word responsible for administering a variety of law enforcement initiatives, including helping to deter, disrupt, and dismantle transnational criminal and terrorist organizations that pose a threat to the American people," the DHS said. "The country of Israel does not assist in the deportation of Iranian nationals." Middle East Eye has contacted the Israeli foreign ministry for comment but received no response by the time of publication. “We know there’s Israeli influence in our policing, in our surveillance state, and Israel does provide a lot of training and support to law enforcement in the United States,” Abdi said. According to Abdi, ICE officials had informed US authorities that it would be difficult to organise deportation flights to Iran because the country’s airspace was closed due to the war. Nevertheless, the White House instructed ICE that this was a top priority. “The decision to send those people back was made as the US and Israel were bombing Iran, and so there was not a disconnect between the fact that we were bombing a country and planning to send vulnerable people back there,” he said. "This is an administration that is unable to distinguish between a war on Iran versus a war on people who are Iranian, and they have been at war with Iranian people for many years.” War on Iran News Post Date Override 0 Update Date Mon, 05/04/2020 - 21:19 Update Date Override 0

Afridi invites people from across country to join PTI's long march at Swabi Interchange on Oct 11. PESHAWAR: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi invited people from across Pakistan to reach the Swabi Interchange on Oct 11, where the PTI plans to announce the next steps for its long march that is being carried out to demand the release of jailed party founder Imran Khan. The route plan for the march has undergone multiple changes since its launch on Oct 4. While the party initially vowed to march towards Islamabad, its final destination seemingly remains tentative as the KP CM has yet to announce the plan for the trek after Oct 11, beyond Swabi. So far, the march has remained within KP, where the PTI is in power. CM Afridi briefly also addressed participants on the way to Charsadda and told them not to worry as “we have to go elsewhere as well after Swabi”. Afridi termed the federal government’s warnings “empty threats” and told the march participants that it “cannot harm the workers after they will cross the province’s boundary”. The PTI march began after weekend talks with the federal government failed to bridge their differences for multiple reasons , particularly over the counterterrorism policy. The federal ministers have warned the PTI not to lead the march beyond KP, and are also linking differences over the counterterrorism policy with the possibility of an emergency or governor’s rule in KP. In his address after reaching Charsadda, CM Afridi said convoys from Peshawar and Malakand divisions would reach the Swabi Interchange on Oct 13, while a course of action for Hazara Division would also be announced on the same day. Convoys from Kohat Division would also reach the Swabi Interchange, while convoys from Bannu and Dera Ismail Khan Divisions would join the march along the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor route, he said, according to a statement issued by his office. The CM urged the people to play their role in the “struggle for Haqiqi Azadi and sovereignty”. He said he wished to place before the public a record of the past years, detailing the performance of the federal government following Imran’s ouster as the prime minister in 2022. “Following the regime change operation, Pakistan’s economic indicators have been showing a negative trend. Pakistan has risen to the top of the Global Terrorism Index, and the country is now bearing the consequences of decisions taken behind closed doors,” he remarked. According to Afridi, 14,000 intelligence-based operations and 22 major military operations have been conducted in KP between 2004 and 2026. “Yet, terrorism has not been eliminated,” he said. He said the people of KP, along with police and military personnel, were “making daily sacrifices and embracing martyrdom”. CM Afridi added, “Whenever I spoke about formulating a policy to eliminate terrorism, my recommendations are not given due consideration.” The CM also decried the alleged non-provision of funds from the Centre to KP. Kundi’s challenge Earlier in the day, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi challenged PTI protesters to dare and cross Swabi, a KP district that borders Punjab’s Attock and which the opposition party in the Centre has announced as the eventual destination of its long march.. Kundi raised doubt on the realisation of the PTI’s plan to reach Swabi on Oct 11. “They are probably going to Charsadda today, then they might go to Mardan, and after that they might end up reaching Afghanistan through Dir,” he said while addressing a press conference in Peshawar. “Because whenever they turn towards Swabi, their legs start shaking, and their hearts tremble […] If they have any self-respect, reach Swabi tomorrow and cross it, or even step inside it. I will accept that you are a revolutionary party that aims to make a naya (new) Pakistan.” Continuing to rail against the party, he said senior PTI leaders were “sitting in drawing rooms” in Islamabad while others were in “hiding”. “They say that they have run successful mobilisation campaigns across Sindh and Punjab; did you see anyone from these provinces on their long march’s truck?” he questioned. Reacting to the PTI’s claims that KP lawmakers and cabinet members were being “abducted”, Kundi said: “You (KP CM Afridi) should tell who is abducting your ministers as you are the chief executive of the province. “You cannot protect your ministers, MPAs, and MNAs; how will you protect my people, the province and the nation? This is your position.” Kundi added that the KP CM and his cabinet should resign on “ethical grounds”. “They say that the SHOs do not listen to them; if no one listens to you, then why are you sitting [in the government]? Only to make money or for corruption,” he remarked, adding that presently, doctors, teachers, nurses, and municipal officers were observing strikes in KP. The KP governor vowed that “we will protect our province and fight against terrorism on the front line. We will show such incompetent people […] how a province is run.” Answering a question, Kundi contended that no province could run without the Centre. “But these people talk about confrontation with the federal government,” he said. On the possibility of governor’s rule or an emergency in KP, the governor said that when the president or the prime minister deems that the situation in the province has worsened to the extent that these options should be availed, they would make a decision. “Whenever the federal government will seek report on province’s situation; we will provide as per the information we have,” he added. In response to another question, Kundi took a jibe at the PTI, saying the party had turned its long march into “Lucky Irani Circus, travelling from city to city […] But whenever they turn to Swabi, they opt to take a U-turn”. He also commented on his recent meeting with KP’s chief secretary and inspector general (IG) to discuss the province’s law and order situation. The KP CM has taken strong exception to the meeting and called for legislation to provide for the governor’s impeachment for “violating the Constitution”. Kundi defended the meeting, saying: “I called the chief secretary and IG because we have no government on the ground in the province; they are busy in their circus.” “My province is burning,” he continued, citing recent incidents of terrorism in KP. “They (PTI) have never condemned terrorism. They cannot challenge the terrorists […] They don’t have any plan to fight terrorism,” he claimed. He added that “terrorism is our red line,”, adding, “We cannot hand over this province to terrorists. This is our point agenda […] we will first talk about terrorism, and other things will follow.”

K-Electric may have to carry out load management as 'extreme' measure during peak hours at night. Power utility for Karachi, K-Electric, said on Friday that it may need to undertake load management as an “extreme, last-resort measure” during evening and night peak hours due to a shortage of re-gasified liquefied natural gas (RLNG), caused by disruptions to global supply and delayed cargoes. “Due to a nationwide RLNG constraint stemming from international supply disruptions and delayed cargoes — affecting generation across the country including KE’s territory — KE may need to undertake load management as an extreme, last-resort measure during evening/ night peak hours, if necessitated. Daytime supply will remain largely stable,” KE spokesperson Imran Rana posted on X. He said KE was in “close coordination” with Pakistan LNG Limited and other authorities to ensure an “early normalisation” and apologised for the inconvenience. A similar situation occurred earlier this year, with consumers across the country facing electricity load management attributed to the unavailability of RLNG. Apologising in August, the government assured them that load management would be reduced “as soon as” the delayed RLNG cargoes arrived. The government had also apologised to power consumers in April for loadshedding exceeding the promised 2.25 hours , arising out of lower water availability for power generation. Pakistan has been grappling with a fuel shortage due to hostilities in the Middle East, which have resulted in disruption of major oil and gas supply routes — the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab — and caused fuel prices to rise. Authorities are struggling to finalise the liquefied natural gas (LNG) import plan for the upcoming three winter months — December to February — amid a challenging supply situation stemming from the US-Iran conflict. Gas companies and the Petroleum Division had sought at least 22 import cargoes for the three-month period, but the task force on energy, led by Lt Gen Zafar Iqbal, has promised no more than 10-12 cargoes of around 100 million cubic feet each on a best-effort basis, using all diplomatic and logistical channels. The plan will be presented to the prime minister for approval, given the involvement of around $100m per spot cargo and the requirement for consent from the Ministry of Finance and the State Bank of Pakistan. Sources, meanwhile, indicate that actual LNG imports may not exceed seven to eight cargoes over the three winter months, given prevailing market conditions, which would bring the outcome closer to the Ministry of Finance’s desired level.

The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

Dreamliners to join PIA fleet next month. Nepra clears use-of-system charges for competitive power market. ISLAMABAD: The Nat­ional Electric Power Reg­ulatory Authority (Nepra) on Friday notified use-of-system charges (UoSC) ranging from Rs6.23 to Rs19.62 per unit for bulk power consumers (BPCs) of all distribution companies, including K-Electric, participating in the competitive electricity trading market. Under the Competitive Trading Bilateral Contract Market (CTBCM), open-access consumers participating in the upcoming 400MW auction will have to pay Rs6.23 to Rs19.62 per unit to use the national grid for transporting electricity from the supplier to the consumer. The UoSC includes transmission and distribution charges, a fixed grid charge and cross-subsidy. A B-3 industrial consu­mer will be charged Rs6.23 per unit, while a B-4 industrial consumer will pay Rs9.09 per unit. These charges will be in addition to the electricity supply price, including generation cost, to be agr­eed between the private-sector supplier and the BPC. At present, there are a little over 3,000 BPCs across the country. The UoSC for C-3 and C-2 single-point distribution consumers has been notified at Rs14.95 to Rs19.62 per unit, while A-2 and A-3 general supply consumers will be charged Rs19.14 per unit. Agricultural consumers will pay Rs6.72 per unit. For BPCs not participating in the competitive wheeling auction, UoSC rates have been set significantly higher, ranging from Rs19.17 to Rs32.56 per unit, depending on the consumer category. In this category, B-3 and B-4 consumers will pay Rs19.17 and Rs25.45 per unit, respectively, while C-2 and C-3 consumers will be charged Rs31.30 and Rs32.56 per unit. A-2 and A-3 consumers will pay Rs32.08 per unit, while agricultural consumers will be charged Rs19.66 per unit. A fixed grid charge of Rs1 per kilowatt per month, based on sanctioned load, will also apply to both categories, irrespective of whether they participate in the competitive auction. The commercial market operation date for the CTBCM had already been declared as Jan 22, 2026, with the first market auction originally scheduled for June. However, the auction was delayed because UoSC charges had not been determined and notified. The notification of uniform UoSC rates for all distribution companies and K-Electric is intended to pave the way for the formal launch of the competitive wholesale electricity market. The Independent System Operation (Ismo), a new power division entity, is expected to auction 400MW of electricity in the first phase within the next couple of months. The government has allocated a total of 800MW for auction in two phases. Nepra had forwarded its UoSC determination to the government for uniform application after considering the views of the power division, Ismo, K-Electric and BPCs on the mechanism for calculating and settling the charges, including inter-Disco differentials, cross-subsidies and transmission and distribution losses. Under government directives, the impact of inter-Disco differentials arising from uniform UoSC rates will not be borne exclusively by wheeling consumers. Nepra had also circulated a draft adjustment mechanism for settling inter-Disco differentials among relevant stakeholders. The regulator said the key principle was to ensure that UoSC applicable to open-access consumers remained equal to those applicable to similarly pla­ced consumers of suppliers of last resort (SOLRs). Based on the transmission and distribution losses of individual Discos, Nepra determined a uniform loss factor of 8.04pc at the 11kV level. For consumers connected at 132kV, it approved a uniform loss factor of 1.51pc, as proposed by the power division. Nepra ruled that any additional charge required to cover differentials among Discos or K-Electric would apply to all consumers, including open-access consumers and those of SOLRs, thereby maintaining uniformity. The federal government had earlier approved framework guidelines for the competitive wheeling auction of 800MW of electricity and for moving towards integrated energy planning across the country. Under the framework, 800MW of generation capacity will be sold through competitive auctions for five years. The quantum could gradually increase after the initial trial, subject to government approval. Ismo will now hold the first 400MW auction under a process approved by Nepra a few days ago. It is also expected to announce the auction calendar and detailed procedure shortly. There will be no upper or lower limit on bid values, which will remain fixed for one year. According to timelines set under the IMF programme, approval of the auction guidelines had been targeted for December, while approval of uniform wheeling charges by Nepra was due in January 2026. World Economic Forum presents case for ‘administrative redesign’ in Pakistan. ISLAMABAD: As Pakistan’s population continues to grow, potentially reaching 265 million by 2030, the World Economic Forum (WEF) has emphasised the need to redesign the country’s administrative geography to promote decentralisation and improve governance. The WEF’s Centre for Regions, Trade and Geopolitics argues that creating more administrative units can lead to better governance, but the broader principle is that institutional geography must evolve when the scale of governance no longer matches the scale of society. There is no universal answer or ideal number of provinces, states or counties, it maintains. However, it adds that when populations grow faster than institutions, governments must be willing to redesign them so that decisions, resources and accountability are brought closer to the people affected by them. A modest reform could divide each existing province into four, creating 16 first-tier governments and reducing the average population per unit from about 60m to roughly 15m, according to the centre. Forum notes that new units can do better only with capable institutions, transparent fiscal transfers The debate in Pakistan, however, should not be framed as a contest over one “correct” map, but as a choice among different governance scenarios. More ambitious models could create 23 to 25 units based on population balance or geographical coherence. Another approach could build on existing administrative divisions, creating more than 30 units, with ave­rage populations closer to those of other large federations, the centre suggests. The centre maintains that each scenario involves trade-offs. Fewer, larger units may be easier to legislate for and finance, whereas a greater number could bring provincial capitals, budgets and political authority closer to citizens though entailing higher transition costs and requiring stronger administrative capacity, it explains. Evidence from other countries also cautions against treating boundary ref­orm as a cure-all. New administrative units can improve responsiveness only when accompanied by capable institutions, transparent fiscal transfers, comparable performance data and incentives for local revenue mobilisation. Provincial revenue collection The centre says Pakistan’s provinces now shoulder major service-delivery responsibilities, yet their own-source revenue remains limited. In 2024-25, provincial taxes generated just Rs983 billion, equivalent to less than 0.9pc of GDP. Agriculture accounts for 24pc of value added, but taxation of agricultural income has historically yielded little revenue relative to the sector’s size. The IMF estimates agriculture’s effective tax rate at just 0.3pc, while agricultural income tax revenues have remained below expectations even after rates were increased in 2025. For decades, provincial tax authorities have struggled with limited administrative capacity, weak enforcement and inadequate information, making it difficult to identify and collect taxes on agricultural income. Recent reforms seek to address some of these weaknesses, but their success will depend on improved data-sharing with the Federal Board of Revenue, greater automation and stronger provincial capacity to enforce the rules. Weak local revenue systems also undermine accountability because citizens find it harder to connect what they pay with the services they receive. Greater fiscal proximity, if designed carefully, could strengthen that link. “For a country exposed to floods, water stress, rapid urbanisation and youth employment pressures, proximity is not a luxury; it is part of resilience,” the centre says. However, it cautions against pursuing administrative redesign merely to create more units. In some countries, too many weak local bodies, lacking adequate fiscal or institutional capacity, can leave governments fragmented but ineffective. The goal is not simply to multiply administrative units, but to align scale, authority, resources and accountability. Pakistan thus raises a question that many fast-growing economies will increasingly face: when does administrative scale itself become a constraint on development? Gaps, disparities The centre notes that successive governments in Pakistan have taken major steps towards decentralisation in recent decades to keep pace with demographic change. These include the 18th Constitutional Amendment and the seventh National Finance Commission award. However, despite their promise, many decisions remain distant from the communities most affected by them. Lahore district has a population of around 13m, while Harnai district in Balochistan has just 128,000. A policy designed in a provincial capital must therefore cater to vastly different local realities. Disparities are also evident in education. The Planning Commission’s District Education Performance Index found that none of the 134 districts assessed reached the “very high” performance category. Recent household survey data also show that 28pc of children aged five to 16 are out of school nationally, with provincial rates ranging from 21pc in Punjab to 45pc in Balochistan. These gaps reflect the distance between policymakers and districts, budgets and outcomes, and authority and accountability, the WEF centre observes. Published in Dawn, October 10th, 2026

Country’s nuclear safeguards pass first-ever IPPAS security review. • IAEA team calls physical protection regime robust after 12-day review; offers recommendations to tighten security rules and procedures • PNRA, IAEA wrap up five-day workshop on commercial-grade nuclear equipment ISLAMABAD: Pakistan has established a robust nuclear security regime for the physical protection of its nuclear materials and facilities, an International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) team of experts found after concluding a comprehensive 12-day review. IAEA’s International Physical Protection Advisory Service (IPPAS) mission conducted its first-ever evaluation of Pakistan’s legislative and regulatory framework for nuclear security covering nuclear materials and facilities. The mission noted that the security framework was appropriately implemented at the specific nuclear facility visited by the experts. According to an IAEA press release on Friday, the regime is continually improved through periodic reviews, while Pakistan’s well-established capacity-building infrastructure actively benefits national, regional and international expertise in nuclear security. The seven-member mission team was led by Khammar Mrabit, a former director general of the Moroccan Agency for Nuclear and Radiological Safety and Security. It included experts from China, Romania, the Russian Federation, Slovakia and two IAEA staff members. Following their assessment, the team provided recommendations aimed at further enhancing Pakistan’s nuclear security regime and its associated procedures. Several good practices were also identified at both regulatory and facility levels. “The first IPPAS mission in Pakistan is completed successfully, marking the country’s commitment in further enhancing regulatory and operational aspects of its well-established nuclear security regime,” Karine Herviou, IAEA deputy director general and head of the Department of Nuclear Safety and Security, said during the mission’s closing ceremony. “Pakistan’s contribution to building the skills of the nuclear security workforce is commendable and has a far-reaching impact.” Hosted by the Pakistan Nuclear Regulatory Authority (PNRA) at the government’s request, the mission aimed to assist the state in strengthening its national nuclear security regime. “Hosting the IPPAS mission underscores Pakistan’s unwavering commitment to maintaining a robust nuclear security regime across facilities and activities,” said Zia Hussain Shah, chairman of the PNRA. “The valuable insights provided by the international experts’ team not only validate our robust physical protection measures but also offer an excellent baseline to further strengthen our legal and regulatory framework, national nuclear security regime, including facility-level practices.” IPPAS missions provide peer advice on implementing international instruments and IAEA guidance regarding the protection of nuclear materials. During these missions, international experts observe a nation’s physical protection systems, compare them with international good practices and make recommendations for improvement on a nationwide and facility-specific basis. The IPPAS team met with officials from the PNRA, the Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission and other relevant national stakeholders. They also visited the Kanupp Decommissioning Project at the Karachi Nuclear Power Generating Station, Pakistan’s first nuclear power plant. The Canadian Deuterium Ura­nium reactor operated from 1971 until its permanent shutdown in 2021. The visit allowed the team to observe ongoing decommissioning activities and spent fuel storage. Pakistan is a party to the Convention on the Physical Protection of Nuclear Material and ratified its 2005 amendment in 2016. This amendment significantly broadens the original scope, establishing obligations to ensure the physical protection of all peaceful nuclear facilities and materials during domestic use, storage or transport. Nuclear safety workshop Meanwhile, the Pakistan Nuclear Regulatory Authority, in collaboration with the IAEA, successfully concluded a five-day National Workshop on Commercial Grade Item Dedication for nuclear safety-related applications. Organised by the National Institute of Safety and Security, an IAEA Collaboration Centre, the workshop concluded on Thursday. It brought together regulatory staff, nuclear installation operators and supply chain stakeholders to discuss a process used when commercially manufactured items are considered for safety-related applications. Speaking on the occasion, PNRA Executive Member Shahid Rashid emphasised the importance of reliable and qualified equipment for the safe operation of nuclear installations. “Factors such as technological advancement, equipment obsolescence and the evolving global supply chain can affect the availability of specialised nuclear-grade components,” Mr Rashid stated. “Commercial Grade Item Dedication provides an important mechanism for establishing confidence that commercially available items can meet the requirements for intended use in nuclear installations.” The PNRA noted the workshop contributed to strengthening Pakistan’s capabilities in nuclear safety and supply-chain oversight, aligning strictly with applicable requirements and international good practices. Remittances rise 14pc to $10.9bn in July-Sept. • UK records the highest growth among major sources, with inflows rising 19.4pc • Saudi Arabia remains the largest source, contributing $2.686 billion KARACHI: Workers’ remittances increased by 14 per cent in the first quarter of FY27 compared with the same period of the previous fiscal year, according to data released by the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) on Friday. However, remittance inflows declined slightly by 1.9 per cent in September compared with August of the same year. The growth trend could help the government achieve its annual remittance target of $44 billion for FY27. “Workers’ remittances were recorded at $3.6 billion during September 2026. In terms of growth, remittances increased by 12.7pc on a year-on-year basis and decreased by 1.9pc on a month-on-month basis,” the SBP said. The seven-month Gulf war did not appear to have significantly affected remittance inflows, despite earlier concerns. Millions of Pakistanis have been working in Gulf countries for years, making their remittances a major source of support for the national economy. Remittances continue to exceed export earnings, despite what the government describes as incentives for exporters. Exporters, however, dispute this assessment, arguing that heavy taxation has weakened the export sector. The latest data show that workers’ remittances rose by 14pc to $10.9 billion during the first quarter of FY27, compared with $9.5bn received in the corresponding period of the previous fiscal year. The increase provides some relief to the government as Pakistan continues to face economic challenges and seeks to meet the conditions attached to its International Monetary Fund (IMF) programme. The IMF pushes for sustainable economic growth but appears less concerned about the resulting increase in poverty. Meanwhile, the World Bank said this week that 48pc of Pakistan’s population lives below the poverty line, despite the country’s adherence to IMF guidelines. However, the impact of remittance growth on the broader economy remains constrained by Pakistan’s rising trade deficit, which offsets some of the benefits of these inflows, including their contribution to the external account. UK remittances up 19.4pc Among major sources of remittances, inflows from the United Kingdom recorded the highest growth rate, rising by 19.4pc to $1.643bn during July-September FY27 compared with the same period last year. Saudi Arabia remained the largest source of remittances, with inflows reaching $2.686bn, representing growth of 16.2pc during the quarter. Remittance inflows from almost all major destinations recorded positive growth during the first quarter of FY27. The United Arab Emirates (UAE) contributed $2.23bn, marking an increase of 12.6pc. Inflows from European Union countries amounted to $1.4bn, up 9.8pc, while Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries, excluding Saudi Arabia and the UAE, contributed $1bn, representing growth of 11.7pc. The major sources of workers’ remittances during September 2026 were Saudi Arabia ($899 million), the UAE ($748.5 million), the UK ($515.1 million) and the United States ($305.9 million). Trial courts can reject time-barred suits on their own initiative: SC. • Courts should nip vexatious litigation in the bud to save judicial time, says Justice Mazhar • SHC order in Askari IV bungalow case set aside • Trial court directed to decide civil suit’s maintainability after giving both parties adequate opportunity of hearing ISLAMABAD: The Supreme Court has ruled that a trial court can reject a palpably vexatious or time-barred lawsuit on its own initiative at the earliest stage, without waiting for a formal application from the defendant. “There is no bar or embargo under Section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1908, or Order VII, Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC), 1908, preventing a court from dismissing a suit or rejecting a plaint on its own initiative, without a formal application from the defendant, if it is barred by law,” observed Justice Muhammad Ali Mazhar while heading a three-judge SC bench that took up an appeal against a Sindh High Court (SHC) order. The case concerned a dispute over a house in Army Officers Housing Colony, Askari-IV, on Rashid Minhas Road in Karachi. The original plaintiffs, including Abdul Wahab Shah, had filed a suit seeking a declaration, possession and partition. In September 2024, the trial court rejected their plaint, ruling that the suit was barred by limitation. The plaintiffs challenged the decision before the SHC, which set aside the rejection order and directed that all pending applications, including one seeking amendment of the plaint, be decided together. The defendant, Muhammad Islam Badshah, then challenged the high court’s decision before the SC. In an eight-page order, Justice Mazhar observed that a court’s power to reject a plaint did not always depend on an application under Order VII, Rule 11 of the CPC. The powers conferred by Section 3 of the Limitation Act were broader in cases where a suit was found to be time-barred, allowing the court to dismiss it and bring the proceedings to a close. A court was responsible for dismissing fundamentally flawed suits to save judicial time and prevent unnecessary litigation, without conducting a mini-trial or examining the written statement, the judge said. If a plain reading of the plaint showed that it was palpably vexatious or meritless, the trial court could invoke Order VII, Rule 11 of the CPC to terminate sham litigation at the earliest stage. This applied where the plaint disclosed no actionable legal right or injury constituting a cause of action, or where the suit was expressly barred by an applicable statute or law, the judgment stated. The court could exercise this power even before issuing summons to the other side, thereby saving judicial time and shielding parties from vexatious and misconceived litigation, Justice Mazhar emphasised. Before rejecting a plaint, however, the court must examine whether it discloses a cause of action; whether the relief claimed is undervalued and, if so, whether the plaintiff has failed to correct the valuation within the prescribed time; and whether the relief is properly valued but the plaint is written on insufficiently stamped paper, with the plaintiff failing to supply the required stamp paper within the time allowed. The court must also determine whether the suit appears, from the statements in the plaint, to be barred by law, the judgment said. The underlying principle is that ineffectual and unproductive lawsuits should be disposed of at the outset so that judicial resources can be devoted to serious and genuine disputes. At the same time, courts should not allow procedural manoeuvres designed to delay proceedings. A meaningful reading of the plaint is essential to reach a just conclusion, the judgment added. If a suit is inherently incompetent because of an express or implied legal bar, rather than a formal, technical or curable defect, it should not be allowed to burden judicial proceedings further. However, the law does not permit the rejection of a plaint in parts. If even one prayer is maintainable, the entire plaint cannot be rejected. Where questions of law and fact are intertwined, the suit should proceed to the written statement and discovery stages. The court may then determine the dispute by framing preliminary issues or conducting a regular trial, ensuring both parties have an equal opportunity to present their cases. The proper course in such matters is to frame issues and decide them on merit in light of the evidence. Courts must ensure substantial justice and avoid leaving parties without a remedy, the judgment held. Concluding the order, the SC directed the trial court to decide the maintainability of the civil suit in accordance with law after giving both parties an adequate opportunity of hearing, and then proceed further. The SC also set aside the SHC’s Feb 6, 2025, order to the extent that it directed the question of maintainability to be decided alongside the application seeking amendment of the plaint.
