Sri Lankan doctor joins efforts to save elephant Madhubala in Karachi. KARACHI: Sri Lankan wildlife health specialist and veterinarian Dr Buddhika Bandara joined Four Paws’ expert Dr Amir Khalil and the Safari Park vet team on Friday to carry out a joint medical examination of the ailing elephant Madhubala. The foreign experts have been invited by local authorities after Safari Park vets failed to diagnose the factors behind Madhubala’s ongoing health crisis. The female African elephant has experienced drastic weight loss in recent months and collapsed twice in her enclosure. “Multiple bacterial and parasitic infections and the weakness that followed treatment for tuberculosis have caused Madhubala to lose significant weight. Additionally, she seems to suffer from a linear fracture in the carpal joint,” explained Dr Amir Khalil of Four Paws to journalists at a press talk organised at the Safari Park. He emphasised the need for better care and management. “Foreign and local vets are working together to save Madhubala as we have been in contact with each other for the past several weeks. Still, there is a need for more efforts,” he said, adding that though she had shown recovery signs, it’s hard to say anything with certainty about her future. Sources said the foreign experts would also examine Malika, Madhubala’s only companion. They are the country’s last two captive elephants. Madhubala had been in solitary confinement at Karachi Zoo following the tragic death of her companion Noor Jehan, who died in 2023 after a fall in her enclosure. Noor Jehan’s autopsy report released by the Karachi Metropolitan Corporation showed that she died from a severe blood parasitic infection and internal trauma combined with a lack of proper medical care. Left alone at the zoo, Madhubala was successfully relocated to Safari Park, where she was reunited with her sisters, Sonia and Malika, in November 2024, under the supervision of Four Paws, which had worked extensively with the KMC for elephant care. The success story of her reunion faded soon after Sonia died a month later after collapsing in her Safari enclosure. Lab reports later showed that she suffered from multiple chronic illnesses, affecting almost all vital organs, indicating prolonged neglect in her care and failure in timely diagnosis. Trump sows doubt on plan to livestream US military execution. US President Donald Trump has cast doubt on whether authorities will livestream the firing squad execution of the perpetrator of a deadly attack on American soldiers, a plan that has drawn broad and bipartisan condemnation , it emerged on Saturday. Nidal Hasan’s execution — scheduled for December 3 at Fort Hood, Texas, where he gunned down 13 people in 2009 — is set to be the first by a US military firing squad since 1945. A Pentagon official told AFP on Thursday that the execution would be streamed live, after US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said: “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public.” But Trump, who supports the death penalty in this case, left it uncertain whether the execution would be publicly broadcast. “They are making a determination about that, but he will be killed,” Trump said. “I really don’t care how he goes, as long as he goes.” Earlier Friday, Vice President JD Vance told journalists who asked about the planned livestream that he does not “know that that’s actually going to happen.” “This is a guy who committed, in my view, the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11,” Vance said, but added that if the execution is broadcast live, “I’m not going to be watching it.” Senator Mark Kelly, a Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Hasan should “face justice” but that public executions are “the kind of thing Iran and the Taliban do. Is this who we want to be associated with?” Tech firms YouTube, Meta and X did not immediately respond to requests for comment on whether they would allow the execution to be streamed on their platforms. TikTok directed AFP to its policy banning depictions of “graphic incidents and violence” including “the shooting of an individual.” The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights condemned the plan, saying in a message sent to AFP on Friday that “the livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture.” Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, said it was a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered.” ‘Compound the cruelty’ Hegseth said it would be the military’s first firing squad execution since World War II. “People need to understand that… there’s serious consequence for these types of things,” Hegseth said in a video shared Thursday on official Pentagon X accounts. The last US military execution was carried out in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged for rape and attempted murder. The Death Penalty Information Centre says 135 troops have been executed by the US military since 1916. According to rights group Amnesty International, at least 17 public executions are known to have been carried out in 2025 — six in Afghanistan and 11 in Iran. Amnesty’s Justin Mazzola said Friday that the death penalty is “a violation of human rights,” and that streaming Hasan’s execution “would only compound the cruelty.” Twelve of the 13 people Hasan killed and 30 of those he wounded were soldiers. He was shot by a civilian police officer who responded to the attack and is paralysed from the waist down. Hasan chose to conduct his own defence during the trial but called no witnesses and gave no testimony, and made no attempt to deny the charges. He was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013. Court-appointed defence attorneys expressed concern that he was seeking execution. The court that convicted Hasan was told he was opposed to the US military’s occupations of Iraq and Afghanistan, and that he had spoken online with an alleged Al-Qaeda figure, radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaki, an American citizen subsequently killed in a US drone strike in Yemen.

‘Betrayal of international law’: US sanctions on ICC draw widespread condemnation. US President Donald Trump’s administration imposed sanctions on the ​International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize , putting Washington on a diplomatic collision course with European allies. The court denounced the move as an “assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order” and called on its 125 member states to take action to defend it. “The Court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it,” the ICC said in a statement, adding that the issue was about safeguarding the international order grounded in the rule of law. “The Court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes,” it said. The move drew widespread condemnation from governments, human rights activists and international organisations, including the United Nations. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the US announcement of sanctions against the ICC as an institution. In a statement, he said “accountability for international crimes and the delivery of justice to victims were central to the global commitment to peace, security, human rights and fundamental freedoms”. UN Guterres reiterated his unwavering support for the independence of the court and its officials. The foreign ministry of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom issued a joint statement opposing the sanctions. “As committed supporters of the ICC we regret and strongly disagree with the announcement of sanctions to be imposed upon the Court by the United States,” the statement said, as shared by Germany’s Foreign Office on X. The ministers also welcomed the court’s preparations to ensure it could continue to fulfil its mandate under the Rome Statute, reaffirming their support for its work. Japan also issued a statement backing the court, joining the other countries in opposing the US move and reiterating its support for the ICC’s ability to carry out its mandate. Belgium condemned the sanctions, saying “the ICC must be able to operate independently”. It called for the activation of the European Union’s Blocking Statute to protect the court. Human rights advocates warned that the sanctions threatened justice for victims of abuses in Palestine, Ukraine, Myanmar and Sudan, describing the move as “an unprecedented assault on global justice and the rule of law”. European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas described the ICC as the “cornerstone of the international criminal justice system”. She said she had spoken with ICC President Tomoko Akane following Washington’s announcement, adding that the six-month period before the sanctions take effect offered an opportunity for dialogue. “The EU has always supported the Court, and the EU has options to ensure that it can continue its vital work,” Kallas said, adding that protecting the ICC remained an EU priority. The United Kingdom’s Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs also condemned the sanctions in a post on X, saying: “The UK stands with the International Criminal Court and we stand united with our partners in strongly disagreeing with sanctions imposed on the Court. “The ICC must be permitted to continue its critical work holding perpetrators of the most horrific international crimes to account.” Amnesty International Secretary General Agnes Callamard criticised the sanctions, describing the move as “a betrayal” of the principles of international criminal law. In a post on X, she urged European governments to “impose immediately blocking orders” to prevent the sanctions from being implemented on European territory. The US Treasury announced the sanctions with a six-month initial grace period, and some other exemptions that would allow some transactions for telecoms, software, payment of pensions and transactions related to detainees. Rubio said the sanctions had been structured to give the court and its member states an opportunity to address US concerns, and would be adjusted if those demands were not met. Washington has denounced the ICC over arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and ​an investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan, which the ICC says is “deprioritised.

India's 'cockroach' movement chief detained ahead of major protest. Indian police detained the head of the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) online movement on Saturday ahead of a major protest it called against the Election Commission, the party said. Abhijeet Dipke and two other leaders were detained before disembarking from a flight in the capital New Delhi, where the demonstration was due to take place, the youth-led CJP said in a social media post. India deployed thousands of police in its capital and restricted transportation in and around Delhi ahead of mass demonstrations on Saturday demanding the resignation of the country’s election chief over alleged voter-roll irregularities. The protests , called by the youth-led CJP , are the culmination of weeks of opposition mobilisation following allegations of misconduct during a nationwide voter-roll revision. Demonstrations erupted across the country after a newspaper investigation last month alleged misconduct by the Election Commission of India (ECI). The ECI has rejected allegations of impropriety in the “special intensive revision”, saying it was intended to remove duplicate and ineligible voters. Delhi Police personnel stand guard ahead of a protest by the youth-led Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) demanding the resignation of India’s Chief Election Commissioner over alleged “special intensive revision” (SIR) voter-roll irregularities, near the India Gate in New Delhi on October 10, 2026. — AFP Opposition parties and critics say the exercise could disenfranchise voters to the benefit of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Tens of thousands of police officers and paramilitary personnel have been deployed across the capital, with multiple layers of yellow metal barricades blocking roads leading to Jantar Mantar, the usual government-designated protest site. Police have not authorised rallies at the site this weekend. The protests, called by the CJP, are widely seen as a reprise of its mass mobilisation in July, which led to the education minister stepping down over an examination scandal. This time, they are demanding ECI chief Gyanesh Kumar resign. ‘Cannot detain the movement’ The allegations are a fresh challenge for 76-year-old Modi during his third term in office. Authorities have ordered the closure of dozens of metro stations, and cancelled several trains coming to New Delhi. However, the Supreme Court on Friday said some trains must still run and that there should be no blanket closure of metro stations. “The dictator would rather shut down the entire national capital and inconvenience millions of citizens than allow a peaceful protest at a designated protest site,” CJP chief Abhijeet Dipke said on X. “Imagine how many lives would be affected because of this shutdown by Modi.” The CJP, which emerged online as a satirical political movement in May, has accused authorities of intimidating its supporters ahead of the demonstration. The party has said that “at least 10,000 people”, including protesters travelling to Delhi by train, have been detained across the country. Rapid Action Force (RAF) personnel stand guard ahead of a protest by the youth-led Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) demanding the resignation of India’s Chief Election Commissioner over alleged “special intensive revision” (SIR) voter-roll irregularities, in New Delhi on October 10, 2026. — AFP Some people detained in the central state of Madhya Pradesh were taken to hotels, The Hindu newspaper reported. Police have not responded to the party’s broader allegations of mass detentions. “You can detain the people — you cannot detain the movement,” said Neha Bora, who has emerged as a leading face of the current protest. The voter list overhaul, which began in 2025, has led to more than 133 million names being excluded from draft rolls. The exclusions include duplicate entries and people found to have died. The poll body said the exercise identifies fraudulently registered voters and aims to prevent “foreign illegal immigrants” from casting ballots. Critics say the drive has disproportionately affected marginalised and minority communities. Members of Modi’s Hindu nationalist BJP have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls.

Supreme Court releases report documenting judicial, institutional reforms. ISLAMABAD: The Supreme Court of Pakistan (SC) has released its report, “Journey Through Reform and Innovation 2026”, documenting the judicial and institutional reforms undertaken from November 2024 to September 2026. The report provides a comprehensive account of the SC’s reform efforts, highlighting progress in case management, reducing the backlog of pending cases, digital transformation, institutional accountability and public access to justice. It documents the implementation of an 86-point Reform Action Plan, supported by a structured governance mechanism, dedicated working groups and regular reviews of reform initiatives. The report also records measurable progress in judicial performance, including a substantial increase in case disposals, greater focus on long-pending cases, expanded digital services and stronger data-driven performance monitoring. It also highlights key national initiatives advanced through the National Judicial (Policy Making) Committee, including time-bound disposal of prioritised cases, establishment of Model Trial Courts, responsible use of artificial intelligence and the development of judicial analytics. Significant progress has also been made in modernising judicial procedures, improving access to court services and strengthening institutional collaboration. The report further documents initiatives aimed at facilitating litigants, enhancing transparency, expanding international judicial cooperation and promoting a more responsive justice system. The document serves as an institutional record of the reform process, capturing both measurable achievements and the continuing work required to strengthen the efficiency, accessibility, predictability and responsiveness of justice delivery in Pakistan.

Pakistan reaffirms commitment to Saudi security at UN Security Council. UNITED NATIONS: Pakistan has reaffirmed its commitment to Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security at the United Nations Security Council (UNSC), declaring that it would stand “ shoulder to shoulder ” with the kingdom in the face of continued Houthi attacks . Addressing the UNSC’s monthly briefing on Yemen on Friday evening, Pakistan’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Asim Iftikhar Ahmad, condemned attacks on Saudi Arabia and called for an immediate end to the hostilities, invoking the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement and recent decisions of its Strategic Political and Defence Committee. “In line with the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, and recent decisions taken by its Strategic Political and Defence Committee, our commitment to the Kingdom’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security is resolute,” Ambassador Ahmad said, quoting Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s statement issued the previous day . He said Pakistan fully supported Saudi Arabia’s legitimate right to defend its people and protect its cities and vital infrastructure. The ambassador condemned Houthi attacks targeting infrastructure in the Makkah Governorate and the Taibah power distribution station in Madinah. He also recalled Pakistan’s condemnation of attacks on King Khalid International Airport and Abha International Airport that resulted in civilian deaths and injuries. “The Houthi militia must immediately cease these attacks,” he said, reiterating Pakistan’s solidarity with the Saudi leadership and people. “The security and sanctity of the Two Holy Mosques must be respected at all times,” the statement quoted the prime minister as saying. Beyond the security of Saudi Arabia, Ambassador Ahmad reaffirmed Pakistan’s support for Yemen’s sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity, as well as its internationally recognised government. He warned that the intensifying Houthi offensive along Yemen’s western coast and around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait underscored the urgency of protecting maritime security. The envoy called on the Houthis to cease attacks on commercial shipping and urged that freedom of navigation be upheld in accordance with international law. The ambassador also expressed support for UN Special Envoy Hans Grundberg’s efforts to contain the escalation, maintain communication and facilitate a cessation of hostilities. He called for an inclusive, Yemeni-led and Yemeni-owned political process under UN auspices. Addressing the worsening humanitarian situation, Ambassador Ahmad said renewed fighting, including the offensive around Taiz and the attack by Houthi elements on Aden airport, had further exposed civilians and essential infrastructure to danger. He called for safe, rapid and unhindered humanitarian access, adequate funding for relief operations and the protection of civilian infrastructure. Food, fuel and essential commercial supplies, he stressed, must reach all those in need. Pakistan also reiterated its call for the immediate, unconditional and safe release of detained UN, humanitarian and diplomatic personnel. “The council must act with unity and purpose to halt Houthi attacks, safeguard regional security, alleviate suffering and restore a credible path towards a political settlement,” Ambassador Ahmad said. Pakistan, he added, would continue to support efforts towards a peaceful, stable and united Yemen and work to advance lasting peace and stability in the region.

Turkiye social media ban for under-15s takes effect Nov 1. Turkiye on Saturday formally declared a ban on the use of social media for under-15s, scheduled to come into effect on November 1. It has joined a growing number of countries legislating to protect children and teenagers from the harmful effects of online platforms. The official state journal published the decision following the adoption of a law by parliament in April. It stipulates that social media providers must “take the necessary technical and administrative measures, including age verification, to implement” protections for young people. “No service likely to produce an addictive effect in children may be offered.” Countries including Australia have introduced restrictions on social media for children and others such as Britain and France are pushing to do the same. They aim to protect children from digital risks such as screen addiction, lack of sleep, bullying and eating disorders. Rights groups have complained of restrictions on freedom of expression in Turkiye targeting LGBTQ communities , the media and the political opposition. Numerous social media accounts have been blocked in recent weeks.

Islamabad ATC disposes of plea to drop terrorism charges against Imaan, Hadi in security breach case. ISLAMABAD: An anti-terrorism court (ATC) on Saturday disposed of a petition seeking to drop terrorism charges against human rights lawyer Imaan Mazari and her husband, Hadi Ali Chattha, in a case related to the removal of security barriers erected for the English cricket team. The court also sought an explanation, which was provided after a brief adjournment, from jail authorities for failing to produce the accused in person despite a court order. The couple were indicted by the ATC on Tuesday in the case. Both opposed the framing of charges, arguing that they had not been provided copies of the case record or allowed to meet their lawyers. ATC Judge Tahir Abbas Sipra was hearing the case in which the couple have challenged the framing of terrorism charges. Neither accused was initially produced before the court, and no representative of the jail administration appeared to explain their absence. The judge directed prosecution and police officials to contact the jail authorities by telephone to ascertain the reason for their non-production. He also ordered the submission of a written explanation via WhatsApp by 11am. Advocate Aimal Khan requested the court to ensure the personal appearance of both accused, pointing out that an earlier order had directed the authorities to produce them either physically or through a video link. The couple were subsequently produced before the court through a video link. Dr Shireen Mazari also appeared, along with lawyers Zainab Janjua and Aimal Khan. At the outset of the hearing, Judge Sipra inquired about photographs taken during the previous proceedings and imposed a ban on mobile phones inside the courtroom. The restriction was later lifted following a request by court reporters. Advocate Zainab Janjua informed the court that the accused had challenged the framing of charges before the Islamabad High Court (IHC), where their petition was scheduled to be heard on Monday. She requested the trial court to defer proceedings until the high court considered their challenge. “What does it matter? If the framing of charges is set aside, the entire proceedings will come to an end,” Judge Sipra remarked, observing that the challenge before the high court did not automatically prevent the trial court from proceeding. The judge also questioned why the trial had stalled at this stage, noting that superior courts had already dealt with related matters and that a show-cause notice had previously been issued. Janjua questioned the repeated failure of jail authorities to produce the accused despite standard operating procedures governing their appearance. She also sought an adjournment, saying senior counsel Riasat Ali Azad was unavailable. During the video-link hearing, Chattha told the court that he and his wife respected the judge and had regularly appeared before him. Referring to the principle of a fair trial, he said they had learnt from the judge that judicial proceedings could not be conducted without due process. “Why are we not being produced before the court?” he asked, questioning how their right to a fair trial under Article 10 of the Constitution was being protected. He also referred to newspaper reports stating that charges had been framed against them. Judge Sipra asked whether the couple had challenged the framing of charges, observing that the high court could set them aside if they had not been framed in accordance with the law. The judge also directed a prison official to arrange chairs for the accused during their video-link appearance and questioned why they had not been brought to court physically as ordered. He directed the relevant authorities to submit a written explanation by 11am regarding the failure to produce the couple. The court adjourned the proceedings pending the submission of the report by the jail administration. When the hearing resumed, the court disposed of the petition seeking to drop the terrorism charges, saying that this was not an appropriate stage to grant the relief sought without hearing arguments from the lawyers representing the two accused, whose counsel had boycotted the proceedings. During the proceedings, the court noted that, according to the report submitted by the jail authorities following the adjournment, the Islamabad Police had failed to provide an escort to bring Imaan Mazari and Hadi Ali Chattha to court. The court observed that the two accused could not be brought to court because the police had failed to provide the required security. Advocate Janjua said the state was acknowledging that the accused had not been brought to court owing to its own failure to provide an escort. “On the one hand, the state is asking the court to record the witnesses’ statements today, while, on the other, the same state is failing to provide security for Imaan and Hadi to appear before the court,” she remarked. She maintained that the failure to ensure their appearance was undermining the accused’s right to a fair trial. Imaan and Hadi’s rearrest The lawyer couple has been in jail since their arrest on Jan 23 in a case registered against them for protesting outside the Islamabad High Court (IHC) and allegedly manhandling the IHC Bar Association (IHCBA) president. The arrest prompted criticism by rights bodies, politicians and journalists, who stressed the couple’s right to a fair trial. Just a day later, a sessions court sentenced them to 17 years on multiple charges under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (Peca) in a case pertaining to controversial social media posts. The convictions were widely condemned by lawyers and United Nations (UN) experts . On Sept 17, following months of litigation before the courts , the Supreme Court suspended their sentences in the case. The SC ordered their release pending the Islamabad High Court’s final verdict on their appeals against the trial court’s decision. However, the reprieve was short-lived as hours later, Islamabad police arrested the couple again in connection with another case and produced them before an ATC, which sent them to jail on judicial remand. The fresh case in which the two were arrested was registered at the federal capital’s Kohsar police station on March 22 last year on the complaint of City Magistrate Ghulam Murtaza Chandio. Imaan and her husband were accused of chanting anti-government slogans and blocking roads and were nominated by name in the FIR. However, at the time of registration of the case, no section of the Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA) had been added. The FIR included sections 188 (disobedience of an order lawfully promulgated by a public servant), 341 (wrongful restraint), 506 (punishment for criminal intimidation), 353 (assault or use of criminal force to deter a public servant from discharging their official duty) and 186 (obstructing a public servant in the performance of official duties).

Centre done mulling emergency, option to be availed if KP does not cooperate on counterterrorism: minister. Parliamentary Affairs Minister Dr Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said on Friday that the Centre had finished deliberating on the imposition of an emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, warning that it would avail the option if the provincial government did not cooperate on counterterrorism. The minister made these remarks on Geo New s programme ‘ Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Saath ’, during which he also refused to confirm reports that a high-level meeting was expected on Saturday to decide on the imposition of an emergency in KP. “The matter of any decisive meeting is not final, nor has it been notified,” he said. The Centre has warned the PTI-led KP government in recent days of sending it packing through an emergency or governor’s rule as the party goes ahead with a protest march to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan. Federal ministers have cited the security situation in KP in this connection with the possibility of a state of emergency in the province. Regarding the reports that the government was considering implementing an emergency in 12 districts of KP, he said, “The reality is that the government has completed its deliberation regarding the implementation of an emergency. Now it is in the hands of the KP government what role it plays in this regard.” The Centre and law enforcement agencies (LEAs) had to end terrorism in KP no matter what, he said, adding that it would be better if provincial government were to cooperate and play a part in this. “But if they don’t want to get involved, then our other option is that after imposing an emergency, terrorism be wiped out, terrorists be eradicated — and as for that Article 232 … it is for the whole province, not just 12 districts,” he added. On the matter of these districts “extremely affected by terrorism”, Chaudhry said that “extraordinary measures are the need of the hour”. However, when questioned, he categorically stated that the consideration of imposing an emergency had “definitively no relation” to the PTI’s ongoing long march, adding that the simultaneous occurrence of the long march and the mulling of an emergency declaration “could be a coincidence”. Rather, he said, the Centre’s deliberations on imposing an emergency had been ongoing for a long time, as an increasing number of police and LEA personnel were being martyred in the province. He claimed that many efforts had been made to bring the KP government on board to play their role, but they were instead “standing like a wall” in front of the Centre’s peace efforts. “There is a cutoff point, at which one has to decide that the final and decisive elimination of terrorists must be done,” the minister said. Although he said no decision had been made regarding a date for the “cutoff”. Chaudhry continued that the federal government had reached the conclusion that further delay in the fight against terrorism was not possible: “Terrorists cannot be given more time to keep carrying out these actions against citizens’ lives and properties and against LEAs.” However, he emphasised that the final decision had definitely been made to take “decisive action to end terrorism in KP”. The minister added that he had met with Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, who is said to have offered to play a role in breaking the deadlock in negotiations between the PTI and federal government. He stated that this option was present, while noting that the “ball is in the KP government’s court”. “The PTI doesn’t even have consensus within their own party on whether they are ready to appoint Maulana Fazlur Rehman as an arbitrator for talks … so how can negotiations move forward?” he said. He added, however, the door for negotiations and dialogue among political parties “never closes permanently”, and that assurance of cooperation from PTI leadership regarding counterterrorism efforts was the “foundation for a permanent solution”.

Anthropic AI model sent fake murder tip to US police in Philadelphia. An artificial intelligence model developed by Anthropic submitted a fabricated tip about an unsolved homicide to Philadelphia police, authorities said on Friday, criticising the company for taking two months to report the incident. The Philadelphia Police Department said the false submission was made in July through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, a public website where people can share information about unsolved killings. According to Anthropic’s account, as relayed by police, the model was running a test that involved interacting with randomly selected websites when it reached the site and filed false information about an unsolved murder. The AI model presented itself as someone who might have knowledge of the case. The incident echoed other recent cases of unintended behaviour involving AI models, including one where an OpenAI agent undergoing a security evaluation broke out of its testing environment and breached systems at AI platform Hugging Face. Anthropic’s breaches have prompted the White House to mandate that AI companies notify and correct security incidents, news outlet Axios reported citing administration officials. “This notification and remediation process is not optional … It is a critical national security obligation,” White House Super Intelligence Force leaders said in a statement to Axios . The episode heightened concerns about the industry’s increased use of AI agents, systems programmed to take multi-step actions without human supervision. Anthropic published a report on Friday outlining multiple types of “unintended” actions that its models have taken, including the incident involving the Philadelphia Police Department website. The report said other organisations impacted included the White House and other US government agencies. The newly revealed incidents “had minimal real-world impact” and were “significantly less severe” than other cybersecurity incidents previously reported, Anthropic said. ‘Unacceptable’ delay The company outlined four categories of incidents that it found during an internal review of its Claude model: exploiting “basic” coding flaws, submitting forms on websites, bypassing requirements for tokens or fees, and using short URLs to get around other limits. Anthropic has turned off internet access for Claude during all internal testing for now “until we have confirmed that our security and monitoring measures … reliably catch behaviours like these,” the report said. Philadelphia police said the phoney tip, dated July 18, was flagged as spam and never reached the department’s Real-Time Crime Centre for vetting. They added that there was no sign that police systems had been breached or department data compromised. Anthropic discovered the incident on September 28, shut down the automated testing process responsible and added a new validation step for future tests, police said. The company alerted the department on October 7, and the two sides met the following day. “The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable,” the department said. Police said their safeguards had limited the impact, but that these “do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide”. “Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers,” the statement added.

Pakistan and Azerbaijan reaffirm strategic partnership, vow closer economic ties. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday reaffirmed Pakistan’s “deep-rooted, fraternal and strategic partnership” with Azerbaijan during a telephone conversation with President Ilham Aliyev, the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said. According to the PMO, the two leaders reviewed bilateral ties and agreed to translate their strong political understanding into closer economic, investment and commercial cooperation. “The prime minister reaffirmed Pakistan’s deep-rooted, fraternal, and strategic partnership with Azerbaijan, characterised by mutual trust and steadfast support on all issues of core national interest,” it said. Reviewing bilateral ties, both leaders agreed that their exceptional political understanding must now be translated into a strong economic, investment and commercial partnership. PM Shehbaz emphasised that the people of Pakistan held President Aliyev and the brotherly people of Azerbaijan in the highest esteem, the statement said. The two leaders “expressed satisfaction at the growing momentum in their multifaceted cooperation and reaffirmed their shared determination to translate the exceptional political goodwill and understanding into a mutually beneficial economic, investment, and commercial partnership”, it said. The two leaders also discussed progress on ongoing bilateral initiatives, particularly the operationalisation of the Asaan Khidmat Centre in Islamabad , modelled on Azerbaijan’s ASAN Khidmet service delivery system. They described the centre as an example of the practical benefits of bilateral cooperation for the people of Pakistan, the PMO said. At PM Shehbaz’s request, President Aliyev agreed to extend Azerbaijan’s full support and expertise for expanding the Asaan Khidmat network across Pakistan. The prime minister thanked the Azerbaijani president for the gesture, describing it as another manifestation of his country’s enduring friendship and solidarity with Pakistan. The two leaders also exchanged views on the evolving regional and international situation and stressed the need for continued consultations and coordination on matters of mutual interest, the statement read. The prime minister briefed President Aliyev on Pakistan’s diplomatic outreach and efforts to promote peace, dialogue and de-escalation in the region. President Aliyev appreciated Pakistan’s constructive diplomatic efforts to facilitate dialogue and mediation, acknowledging their importance for regional peace and stability, according to the PMO. The conversation concluded with both leaders reaffirming their commitment to strengthening bilateral cooperation and transforming their strategic partnership into a lasting relationship of shared progress and prosperity, the statement added. PM Shehbaz also took to X to post about the telephone conversation. “We reaffirmed the enduring friendship and strategic partnership between Pakistan and Azerbaijan, and our resolve to translate our strong bilateral ties into greater economic, investment and trade cooperation,” he said. The two leaders last spoke by phone on May 12, when they discussed regional developments and efforts to restore peace in the Middle East, while reaffirming the strong fraternal ties between Pakistan and Azerbaijan. PM Shehbaz last visited Azerbaijan in May 2025, when the two leaders pledged to diversify their strategic partnership through investment in mutually beneficial areas. They also reviewed bilateral relations and expressed satisfaction over the growing cooperation between the two countries.

PM Shehbaz, Fazl speak on reducing tensions between federal, KP govts. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday had a telephone call with Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam—Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, with reducing tensions between the Centre and the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government among the topics discussed. According to a statement from the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO), PM Shehbaz congratulated the JUI-F leader on performing Umrah and extended an invitation for talks at the Prime Minister’s House. “Maulana Fazlur Rehman accepted the prime minister’s invitation [and] the meeting is expected to take place soon,” the statement read. The phone call follows recent contacts between Fazl, known for his engagement with politicians from across the board, and the opposition. The Oct 3 talks held to bridge differences between the Centre and the opposition alliance Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-i-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) failed due to multiple reasons , particularly the counterterrorism policy. On Tuesday, TTAP leaders called on Fazl at his residence, following which the veteran politician advised the federal government not to obstruct the PTI long march heading towards Islamabad, as protests were a democratic right enjoyed by all political parties. The next day, PM’s Adviser on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah, Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry and National Assembly Speaker Ayaz Sadiq met the JUI-F chief. On Thursday, PTI MNA Junaid Akbar confirmed that Fazl had offered to play a role in ending the deadlock between the government and opposition, adding that the PTI’s “doors are open” to it. Speaking on Geo News , Akbar had said no framework had been put forward by Fazl regarding his role in the negotiations, although he noted that the JUI-F chief had been in touch with PTI leadership while he was away for Umrah. The same day, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif also hinted at efforts to restart negotiations between the Centre and the opposition, saying, “I wish a positive result comes out of the efforts of those involved in the talks. But, I have little hope.” Speaking to Dawn , JUI-F spokesman Aslam Ghauri said his party chief was playing the role of a “facilitator, not a mediator”. He distinguished the two roles by saying that a mediator would have the authority from opposition parties to make his own decision in light of their demands. “It is our (JUI-F’s) priority to bring both sides on table for resumption of talks,” he added, pointing out that they had urged the government to call a multi-party conference in Parliament House, where political and security issues should be discussed. The JUI-F leader said sitting at the table would benefit both sides, though the resumption of dialogue would mostly benefit the PTI because the KP government is “virtually being run by someone else and not by Chief Minister Sohail Afridi”. Heightened tensions between Centre, PTI The PML-N-led federal government and the KP government led by PTI — which is in opposition in the Centre — have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy. The PTI has said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre has denied . It also calls for reviewing the counterterrorism policy, while the latter criticises the KP government’s efforts to combat terrorism in the province and objects to its stance on dialogue with the Afghan Taliban. Information Minister Attaullah Tarar on Saturday assailed the PTI-led Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government over a “lack of governance” in the province. Addressing a press conference in Islamabad, he alleged that the provincial government was given Rs700 billion under the National Finance Commission for development projects. “You did not upgrade the Counter Terrorism Department (CTD), did not establish forensic labs, did not install safe city cameras, which should be installed in the merged districts and all the entry-exit points of KP’s districts,” he alleged. On the other hand, the information minister claimed that the PTI was spending this money on organising protests. “You don’t even give half an hour to discuss terrorism in the province, but you organise six-hour meetings to spread turmoil and vandalism,” he criticised. Tarar further said that the PTI had “trapped” millions of people in the province to get its leader, former prime minister Imran Khan, released from jail. “You trapped them in poverty, in disease by not providing the adequate health facilities, in ignorance by not providing educational opportunities, and in non-development by not improving infrastructure,” he said. Tarar also alleged that the KP government had held the people of the province “captive to terrorists”. “From the very first day, this is my opinion that they [PTI] are the B-team of the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan,” Tarar said. The information minister said that the PTI facilitated terrorists in settling in the country. “For how long will it go on? That the security forces will clear the area of terrorists and establish peace, but you will bring the terrorists back?” he asked. During his address, Tarar said that the PTI government in KP had dragged the province into the “stone age” during the last 13 and a half years. Citing various federal government projects, Tarar maintained that there was no comparison of the hours spent working by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi to address governance issues and take relief and reform measures. He said that the chief ministers of all the provinces were working hard, questioning how many hours Afridi spent on governance. “Tell us if you have ever given a big hospital, a university, a highway to your people, an information technology project to the youth of KP or given them laptops or gadgets,” he said. “How long can such a system, where there is chaos and extremist politics, continue?” he asked. He claimed that the KP government wanted to hand over the province to terrorists as it prioritised “personal interests over the national interests”. “This province needs peace, not politics,” Tarar stated. Asked about imposing an emergency or governor’s rule in KP, Tarar said that responding to this question would be premature. “Everyone is asking how long KP and its people will remain at the mercy of its government,” he said. “In my opinion, the conditions in KP have never been worse. They could not be worse than this. What’s worse than terrorists roaming in the streets? You have designated no-go areas in most of your districts because you collect ransom in collusion with terrorists,” he claimed. He said that the people of KP go to Punjab or other provinces for medical treatment. “Will there ever come a time when people from across Pakistan go to KP for treatment?” he asked. The information minister asserted that the PTI would not be allowed to destroy the province. Addressing the same press conference, Coordinator to the Prime Minister on Information for KP Affairs Ikhtiar Wali Khan also questioned the lack of development in the province. “Universities are shutting down because there are no vice chancellors there. Eighteen out of 34 universities in KP are on the verge of bankruptcy,” he said. Wali said that people complained about the lack of good roads in Karachi. “But when people of KP go to Karachi, they say that Karachi’s roads are much better than KP.” Calling on the people and journalists in KP, Wali urged them to talk about the “ground realities”, claiming that the people were crying over the existing health facilities in the province. He referred to the KP police as the shuhada force, alleging that the provincial government had left them unarmed. He alleged that the PTI government had seized the money allocated to fund the CTD to combat terrorism. Wali also accused KP ministers of corruption and bad governance in the province. “The people of KP need peace, health facilities and a political culture based on tolerance, acceptance and respect,” he said. This was also a key reason behind the breakdown of the Oct 3 talks between them. The PTI has said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre has denied . Diegograndi Special Coverage / Global 25 September 2026 8 minutes Updates from the UN General Assembly 2026 Marking the opening of the 81st UN General Assembly, Crisis Group experts discuss challenges facing the UN’s efforts to promote international peace and security. This page includes updates from the High-Level Week in New York and recent Crisis Group coverage of the UN. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy World leaders are gathering in New York during the week of 21 September for the UN General Assembly’s annual high-level session. They will find an organisation trapped in an open-ended institutional crisis. UN diplomacy to halt wars and ease civilian suffering is largely paralysed, while a second year of cost cutting has weakened the organisation’s capacity to respond. The UN is in need of revival. Even with these limitations, the UN remains the only universal forum for international cooperation on war and peace, even as the world order it anchors is under mounting strain. Many member states hope that the next Secretary-General, set to be selected by the end of 2026, can help the organisation forge a new direction that enhances diplomacy and deepens respect for international law. A new Secretary-General, regardless of the skills and experiences that she or he may bring to the role, cannot solve the world’s crises overnight. But she or he can and should work with member states to address immediate challenges. High on the list should be bolstering the UN’s peacemaking and conflict management capacities, mobilising political and financial support, and making a renewed case for international cooperation. This special coverage page will feature all of Crisis Group’s work related to the UN General Assembly’s High-Level Week in 2026, as well as its broader work on the UN from the past year. The New Forever War mloukili Tue, 09/29/2026 - 10:38 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Op-Ed / Middle East & North Africa 29 September 2026 1 minutes The New Forever War Originally published in Foreign Affairs Why America and Iran Fight On Without Victory Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Ali Vaez Deputy Program Director, MENA https://twitter.com/AliVaez Related Tags Iran United States When will the war in Iran end? American officials claim that the answer is soon. “I think the war is going to end immediately after the [November] election,” declared U.S. President Donald Trump in September. “They can’t hold out any longer.” Iranian leaders agree that the war’s conclusion is near. Tehran has “brought the most heavily armed army in the history of the world to its knees,” proclaimed Ahmad Vahidi, the commander in chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, in August. Many outside analysts think that the conflict will drag on for longer and end with negotiations rather than with a clear winner. But generally, there is a sense that the fighting will soon be resolved, one way or another. Such thinking is understandable. All wars eventually end, and after months of rising energy prices, the world is especially eager for this one to stop. Yet the unsettling reality is that the conflict is nowhere near over. The war’s two principal belligerents cannot achieve their desired goals, yet they both feel they are accomplishing enough to make continued fighting through a mix of military and economic tools worth it. The United States cannot topple the Iranian regime, get it to give up its missile program, force it to abandon its nuclear program, or make it stop supporting its regional partners. But Washington can keep degrading Iran’s military and constricting its economy. Iran cannot evict the world’s only superpower from the Middle East. Yet it can keep damaging U.S. regional bases, bombing the United States’ regional allies, and disrupting international commerce. The full article can be read on the Foreign Affairs website. South Sudan’s President Jettisons Unity Government and Hardens Grip on Power eschelhaas Tue, 09/29/2026 - 11:07 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Analyst's Notebook / Africa 29 September 2026 2 minutes South Sudan’s President Jettisons Unity Government and Hardens Grip on Power Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech examines how President Kiir’s call for fresh elections aims to weaken his opponents, and may pave the way to worsening armed conflict Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Daniel Akech Senior Analyst, South Sudan https://twitter.com/jongethon Related Tags South Sudan South Sudan’s President Salva Kiir on 22 September dissolved the transitional unity government, established under a 2018 peace deal, declaring that the country would now prepare for long-delayed elections in December. But with the feasibility of holding the polls in doubt and fighting between government and rebel forces continuing in Jonglei and Upper Nile states, the move in effect serves to further concentrate power in the hands of Kiir and his family. Kiir’s move followed the adoption by parliament, which is loyal to the president, of a controversial amendment to the National Elections Act on 21 September, authorising the creation of a caretaker government. This amendment gave Kiir the opportunity to remove his five vice presidents – many of whom were appointed under the 2018 deal, including his perennial arch-rival, First Vice President Riek Machar. The government had already placed Machar, who led the rebel forces in the five-year civil war that ended in 2018, under house arrest in March last year, charging him with treason . State and rebel forces have been fighting since then, threatening to thrust South Sudan back into internecine conflict. Its last civil war is estimated to have cost nearly 400,000 lives and displaced more than four million people. President Kiir further marginalised rival factions and opposition elements in his caretaker government. His newly appointed ministers are almost entirely loyalists, whereas the Nuer – South Sudan’s second-largest ethnic group, to which Machar belongs – remain heavily underrepresented. There are now three Nuer cabinet ministers out of a total of 17, even after the president added additional appointees on 28 September. Kiir also appointed powerful figures from the security forces to become caretaker governors in key states, such as James Koang Chuol in Upper Nile, Moses Majok Gatluak in Jonglei and Rin Tueny Mabor in Lakes. Some political leaders have denounced the unrepresentative make-up of the new administration and rejected the changes. Kiir’s moves set up two potential scenarios. One is a rush to stage-manage snap elections, the first of their kind since the country’s independence in 2011, which could end up re-electing Kiir despite questions as to whether credible polls are even possible without an updated census, voter registry or dedicated funding. A mismanaged vote could also spark fresh rebellions or political violence. Alternatively, Kiir could delay elections yet again on technical grounds, effectively extending his term without the baggage of the 2018 accord’s power-sharing arrangements. Kiir is using an “inter-party dialogue” that started on 24 September to validate plans for elections in December or negotiate such an extension. Either way, Kiir’s moves have triggered alarm among the South Sudanese political elite that his aim is to consolidate power with the goal of managing a dynastic succession . His daughter Adut Kiir is now his most powerful aide, while his son Atem Salva Kiir oversees the presidential guard. Meanwhile, the new rebellion by Machar’s forces looks unlikely to subside as long as its leader remains on trial and under arrest. The U.S.-led Anti-ISIS Coalition is Leaving Iraq: What Happens Next? eschelhaas Tue, 09/29/2026 - 18:14 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Iraqi security forces stand guard during a funerary procession for a slain member of Iraq's Hashed al-Shaabi, or the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), who was killed in a US-Israeli air strike in Mosul the previous evening, in Baghdad on March 8, 2026. AHMAD AL-RUBAYE / AFP Commentary / Middle East & North Africa 29 September 2026 14 minutes The U.S.-led Anti-ISIS Coalition is Leaving Iraq: What Happens Next? The coming withdrawal of U.S.-led coalition forces marks a significant moment in Iraq’s tumultuous recent history. Yet with the Middle East war bringing conflict to the country and questions surrounding the state’s capacity to assert its authority, the significance is mainly symbolic. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Also available in Arabic English Arabic Related Tags Iraq United States On 30 September, the U.S.-led coalition formed to fight the Islamic State (ISIS) is due to end its military mission in Iraq. While some had expected that the withdrawal of personnel and removal of materiel might slip beyond the scheduled date, it now appears that they will be completed on time. The largest remaining contingent is from the United States, which has maintained the biggest troop presence throughout. Several other coalition countries already have pulled out their smaller garrisons, including Poland, which completed its drawdown in March, and Germany , whose soldiers left in August. The departure closes a chapter that began in 2014, when ISIS seized large parts of the country and U.S.-led forces – which had previously invaded and occupied Iraq in 2003 and then withdrawn in 2011 – returned at Baghdad’s invitation. A number of Iraqi armed groups that first formed to combat ISIS came to cast the coalition as a threat. Aligned with Iran, these groups long invoked the coalition’s presence as a justification for keeping weapons and command structures outside the Iraqi state. With coalition forces on their way out, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has declared that these groups must now disarm. But the coalition is leaving amid a Middle East war sparked by U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran, in which Tehran and some of its aligned groups based in Iraq have launched attacks on U.S. targets in Gulf Arab countries, Jordan and Iraq’s own Kurdistan region. The question is whether Baghdad can and will use the end of this foreign military mission to gain greater control of armed actors who – whatever justification they may offer – have reasons for fighting that extend well beyond opposition to the coalition’s presence. The End of a Mission The U.S.-led Global Coalition to Defeat the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria – dubbed Operation Inherent Resolve by the U.S. military – is ending its mission twelve years after its establishment. At that time, in 2014, a marauding ISIS had capitalised on the instability that gripped much of the Arab world following the 2011 uprisings, helped by the acquisition of conventional weapons from Iraqi and Syrian forces that quickly retreated from major cities such as Mosul and Raqqa in the face of the group’s onslaught. It exploited growing sectarian tensions in Iraq and perceptions of political exclusion among its Sunni Arab population to seize much of the country’s Sunni Arab heartland. In June 2014, ISIS declared a caliphate in Iraq and Syria and at its height, in May 2015, controlled as much as a third of Iraqi territory. Having terminated the U.S. occupation of Iraq only three years earlier, then-U.S. President Barack Obama decided to send troops back to prevent ISIS from expanding further and reverse its gains in both countries. In the ensuing years, the U.S. and dozens of coalition partners supported military operations against the group in both Iraq and Syria at the same time as they sought to help rebuild and train the Iraqi army, which had collapsed in a matter of days after the ISIS offensive. While the Iraqi government declared victory over ISIS as early as December 2017, having retaken Mosul and other key cities from ISIS control and secured its border with Syria, the coalition endured. It remained in the country even after March 2019, when the final ISIS stronghold in Baghouz, Syria fell; that loss marked the end of the group’s control of the last bit of the territory it had grabbed since beginning its 2014 offensive. The coalition – which included sizeable contingents from France, the UK and Türkiye in addition to the U.S. – stayed on for several reasons. First, it continued to support Iraqi armed forces suppressing residual ISIS cells for years after the recapture of Baghouz. The Iraqi army and Kurdish region’s armed forces ( peshmerga ) continued to suffer occasional hit-and-run attacks in the so-called disputed territories, an area claimed by both the federal and regional governments, whose rugged terrain offered ISIS fighters plenty of hideouts. As late as August 2024, U.S. troops operating alongside Iraqi forces sustained injuries during a raid on an ISIS cell in Anbar province. Secondly, the coalition used Iraq as a base from which to conduct operations against the group and others across the border in Syria, where a civil war raged for years, and where the U.S. partnered with the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) until April. The ISIS danger appears to have significantly receded. Despite occasional attacks by its remnants, the group has lost its ideological traction. Though some people in both Iraq and Syria continue to harbour the grievances that ISIS played upon to galvanise support, few want to relive the era of the so-called caliphate, which triggered years of conflict and destroyed many of the communities the group ostensibly sought to protect. Moreover, the security gaps that ISIS exploited in 2014 have also narrowed in both countries. Syria’s new authorities have yet to establish full control of the country’s provinces and borders, but the process of integrating the previously autonomous SDF in the north east under the central government’s command is helping secure areas that remain vulnerable to ISIS. In Iraq, state forces are better prepared to repel any domestic or external threat the group might pose. Though the coalition and the Iraqi government share the assessment that Iraqi forces can counter ISIS on their own, the withdrawal is also politically expedient for both Baghdad and Washington. For years, despite its cooperation with coalition forces, Baghdad viewed their presence as a liability, not least because Iran-aligned armed groups seized on it to claim that the U.S. occupation was continuing. Those groups also accused the U.S. of using its foothold in Iraq to monitor Iran and the “axis of resistance” – its partners in the region. This latter charge became a justification for the Iraqi groups to retain their arms and command structures independent from the Iraqi state forces. Domestic political dynamics on the U.S. side may not have been as clear-cut, but they nevertheless militated for withdrawal. Trump was never the pure non-interventionist that he seemed to tout himself as being, but he has long sounded off against the Iraq war (a key theme of his 2016 campaign) and had already considered withdrawing from Syria during his first term. Despite his growing penchant for military intervention in his second term, Trump has continued to inveigh against endless U.S. wars, notably in the Middle East. Departing from Iraq is thus consistent both with the president’s longstanding rhetoric and also the views of significant parts of his political base. To the extent that Washington had contended that the coalition remained in Iraq at its government’s request, Baghdad’s desire for a troop withdrawal has for some time been a complication. Lastly, as a U.S. official noted to Crisis Group, amid the war with Iran, withdrawal would have the added benefit of reducing readily accessible U.S. targets for Tehran. Unlike during the 2011 U.S. withdrawal, Iraqis need not anticipate the next war; it is already affecting the country. In theory, the withdrawal should mark a milestone in Iraq’s relationship with the U.S. and its long road to normalcy following the chaos and violence that have plagued the country since the 2003 U.S. invasion. A series of Iraqi governments have desired to forge bilateral security cooperation agreements on Iraq’s own terms and with countries of its choosing. Baghdad can now strike these deals, not only with the U.S., but also with other former coalition partners such as the UK and France. But however politically necessary it may have deemed the withdrawal, Baghdad will hardly be able to sell the coalition’s departure as a celebratory moment, given that it coincides with the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, which has turned Iraq into a battleground. Instead, the withdrawal’s timing will focus further attention on that conflict’s spillover effects. Unlike during the 2011 U.S. withdrawal, Iraqis need not anticipate the next war; it is already affecting the country. The fears of many Iraqis are therefore presently not centred around the risk of a resurgent ISIS but rather around Iran-aligned domestic groups that, in solidarity with their “axis of resistance” partners, and notwithstanding the U.S. withdrawal, may take action in defiance of the government’s policy of neutrality in the U.S.-Iran war, and thereby provoke military retaliation by outside actors. Some of the complications that the withdrawal could present for the Iraqi-U.S. relationship would have been difficult to anticipate when the drawdown timeline was conceived. That happened at another tense moment, following the outbreak of the Gaza war, when U.S. backing for Israel’s brutal military response to Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attacks undermined public support for bilateral close ties. In September 2024, when Zaidi’s predecessor Mohammed Shia’ al-Sudani was prime minister and Joe Biden was U.S. president, Baghdad and Washington agreed on a phased end to the coalition’s military mission. It would start with the coalition’s withdrawal from bases in federal Iraq by September 2025, to be followed by the final withdrawal from the Kurdistan region by the next 30 September. Now, with the U.S.-Iran war as backdrop, the withdrawal may well attract less attention as an indicator of the country’s recovery from ISIS than as a test of whether its government can repair Iraq’s battered sovereignty and protect its internal security at a moment of regional crisis. Reining In Armed Groups Zaidi has declared that the end of the coalition mission should mark the beginning of disarmament for groups that operate independently of the state. He has set June 2027 as the deadline for its completion. His political argument is straightforward: once the coalition troops are gone, the armed factions should no longer be able to invoke their presence as grounds for maintaining separate military structures. As he announces the mission’s conclusion on 30 September, he is expecting some of the factions to welcome a development that meets their longstanding demand and to reciprocate with their own commitment to cease hostilities. But not all of the armed groups will do so, given the variations among them and the dynamics created by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. The Popular Mobilisation Forces, or Hashd al-Shaabi, emerged as a collection of Shiite armed groups assembled to fight ISIS and were subsequently nominally incorporated into Iraq’s formal security apparatus, with many retaining independent chains of command. They do not form a single faction and have very different relationships with Tehran. Not all have engaged in attacks outside Iraq’s borders. Some groups, such as Asaib Ahl al-Haq, appear willing to negotiate their future relationship with the state. Others, including factions associated with the self-described Islamic Resistance in Iraq, such as Kata’ib Hizbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba, are tied ideologically and operationally to Iran’s regional network. Their opposition to the U.S. extends well beyond the presence of coalition troops in Iraq, and they have served as a valuable vector for Iranian power projection. It is these latter factions that have participated in the Middle East war, striking U.S.-linked targets and energy infrastructure in neighbouring countries, including Jordan, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia. Their actions have strained Baghdad’s relations with Gulf states and, as noted, exposed Iraq to military retaliation by both the U.S. and Saudi Arabia. Zaidi thus has good reasons of his own to want to curb them, as his government cannot credibly reassure its neighbours, attract investment or pursue a foreign policy of neutrality while armed actors make decisions on war and peace independently of its will. Negotiations under way with individual groups offer a possible, albeit incremental, pathway to bringing personnel and capabilities under state command. Negotiations under way with individual groups offer a possible, albeit incremental, pathway to bringing personnel and capabilities under state command. They also are almost certain to take far longer than Zaidi’s deadline allows. If the talks stall, Zaidi could face U.S. pressure to use force against groups that earlier prime ministers were reluctant to confront militarily, fearing an intra-Shiite conflict and friction with Iran. In a mid-September interview , Zaidi said groups continuing to function as separate militias would be considered outlaws. He has yet to specify what action the government would take to corral those that defy him. As long as Tehran relies on close Iraqi partners in its war with the U.S., these groups have reason to preserve their military autonomy and may seek to prolong negotiations without relinquishing their arms. Even after the coalition’s withdrawal, they will likely point to other foreign security relationships, including Türkiye’s garrison in northern Iraq, to defend their stance. Some have also argued that any disarmament plan must simultaneously address the status of the Kurdish region’s peshmerga, although the parallel is inapt: peshmerga forces are governed by a specific law under the Iraqi constitution regarding federal regions’ responsibility to organise their own internal and border security. The government therefore ought to distinguish between forces operating under recognised state or regional authority, and factions conducting attacks without any such justification. The Kurdish Region’s Vulnerabilities The coalition’s departure has particular significance in the Kurdistan region, where its forces have supported the peshmerga and where U.S. troops remained even after leaving other bases in Iraq in September 2025. Erbil is not happy to see them depart. Regional Prime Minister Masrour Barzani described withdrawal at this moment as “ shameful ”, no doubt because he is concerned about how to manage the threat posed by Iran and Iran-aligned groups, which have systematically targeted the region since the war began in February. Some of the strikes appear to have been motivated by the presence of U.S. forces, in line with attacks on other nearby countries hosting U.S. bases. But the near-daily strikes also have often hit Iraqi-based Iranian Kurdish opposition groups and were described by a Kurdish official to Crisis Group as a warning to Kurdistan to keep those groups out of the current conflict. Certainly, the coalition’s withdrawal will exacerbate vulnerabilities. Coalition forces based in Erbil provided the region with some level of air defence. Their impending departure will mean the loss of those capabilities, further exposing the region to missile and drone attack. The Kurdish official noted to Crisis Group that worries about the withdrawal were “not just about security and protection, but the message this sends to our adversaries”, reflecting fears that Iran and others will see the U.S. drawdown as an indication that they would no longer take a significant interest in the region’s future. Still, U.S. support will not necessarily dry up entirely, even if the basis for it will change. To date, U.S. support for the peshmerga has been governed by a memorandum of understanding between the Pentagon and the Kurdistan Regional Government’s Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs, first signed in 2016 and last renewed in 2022 . But though the U.S. does not wish to extend the agreement, Kurdish authorities will continue to press Washington and other coalition partners for aid in the form of strikes, intelligence sharing, training and equipment – none of which necessarily requires a troop presence inside Iraq – as well as broader reassurance of assistance in facing the military threat from Iran and the groups that it backs. It may help that the regional government announced in September its completion of a peshmerga reorganisation sought by the U.S. and agreed to in the lapsing memorandum. But future cooperation will require further work to define the terms on which Baghdad, Erbil and foreign partners will operate. Erbil and Baghdad, whose relationship has traditionally been fraught, will surely have to work together more closely. That said, at least for now, Kurdish officials say they are impressed with Zaidi and believe he is sincere in his stated intention of trying to tackle the militia problem. Looking Ahead When Trump returned to the White House for his second term, much of his base hoped and believed that his administration would avoid military adventurism and seek to extract the country from strategic quagmires. Some of his personnel decisions, particularly at the Pentagon, seemed to lend credence to such speculation, as did the foreign policy views of his vice president, JD Vance. Officials who sought to pursue a more restraint-oriented foreign policy or to concentrate on competition with China by downsizing other overseas commitments were not a dominant force within the new administration but nevertheless held key positions. Both of these groups favoured reassessing U.S. force posture in the Middle East, particularly the legacy missions in both Iraq and Syria. Whatever influence these camps have, their perspectives have not guided key foreign policy decisions in Trump’s latest year in office, which has been characterised by aggressive unilateralism and reliance on military force as a tool of statecraft. But the trajectory of U.S. policy on Iraq and Syria is an exception to that trend. Administration sources tell Crisis Group that, buoyed by the unexpected ouster of President Bashar al-Assad in Syria, key U.S. officials, particularly at the Pentagon, pushed to reassess the U.S. troop presence there and prevailed in a series of internal policy debates on the matter. Those efforts were boosted when it became clear how vulnerable U.S. troops in the region had become as a result of the conflict with Iran. U.S. officials also have positive views of Zaidi, who visited Washington in July and was received warmly by Trump. They are particularly pleased by Zaidi’s pledges on armed group disarmament. Even those who are sceptical of how those efforts will fare appreciate the Iraqi prime minister’s tone and confidence. What comes next for U.S.-Iraq relations will likely depend on the uncertain trajectory of the U.S. war with Iran. What comes next for U.S.-Iraq relations will likely depend on the uncertain trajectory of the U.S. war with Iran. A prolonged conflict is likely to lead Iran to enlist its partners in Iraq to use the country as a staging ground for significant attacks on the interests of the U.S. and its regional partners. That in turn would inevitably undermine the bilateral relationship and could trigger retaliatory U.S. moves at a time when Washington still enjoys outsized influence, including because it controls a significant portion of Iraq’s oil proceeds, which are deposited in the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The Trump administration has already twice used the leverage the oil revenue affords the U.S. in pressing Iraq to take more proactive measures to dilute Iran’s influence. For now, Zaidi’s ascension has eased strains, and the U.S. withdrawal gives him an argument for reining in armed groups. That may be enough for him to make progress with some of the groups, but doubters are right to question how far he will be able to go. Indeed, it would be entirely unrealistic to expect that Baghdad can compel the surrender of weapons or severing of ties with Iran forged through years of regional conflict. The symbolism of 30 September is significant, but in the end Iraq’s stability will depend more on whether the U.S. gives it the time and space required to bring armed groups under its central authority, and whether Baghdad and Washington work together to protect Iraq from the worst effects of the U.S.-Iranian confrontation in the meantime.
